items.stem: A beam of cosmic-ray muons moves vertically downward at $v = 0.980c$ ($c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$). The mean proper lifetime of a stationary muon is $t_0 = 2.20\,\mu\text{s}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\gamma = 5.03$, $t = 11.1 μs$. (b) $d = 3.25e+3 m$. (c) in Earth frame muon lifetime is time dilated whereas in the muon rest frame atmosphere depth is length contracted.

markScheme.criterion: Computes $\gamma = 1 / \sqrt{1 - 0.980^2} = 5.03$ and multiplies by $2.20\,\mu\text{s}$.
Correct dilated lifetime 11.1 μs.
Multiplies $0.980 c$ by dilated lifetime in seconds.
Correct Earth-frame distance 3.25e+3 m.
States muon lifetime is undilated ($2.20\,\mu\text{s}$) in its own rest frame.
Explains the atmospheric depth is length-contracted by factor $\gamma$ in the muon frame.

parts.prompt: Calculate the mean lifetime of these muons in the Earth reference frame.
Calculate the mean distance travelled by the muons in the Earth frame before decaying.
Explain how an observer moving alongside the muons accounts for their survival over this atmospheric depth.
parts.expectedAnswer: Relativity is frame-consistent because in Earth frame muon lifetime is time dilated whereas in the muon rest frame atmosphere depth is length contracted, so the contracted atmosphere passes within $2.20\,\mu\text{s}$.
workingSteps: In the muon's own rest frame, its lifetime remains the proper time $2.20\,\mu\text{s}$.
The approaching atmosphere is Lorentz-contracted by factor $\gamma$ to roughly $647\text{ m}$, traversable within $2.20\,\mu\text{s}$.

items.stem: In a supernova nucleosynthesis positron-decay sequence, a parent titanium nucleus (A = 44, Z = 22) transforms via purely weak beta-plus transitions (u → d + e⁺ + νₑ) into a final nuclide with A = 44 and Z = 20, conserving baryon and lepton numbers at every vertex.
items.workedSolution: (a) ΔZ = 20 − 22 = −2. Final answer: −2. (b) N₀ = 44 − 22 = 22; N_f = 44 − 20 = 24. ΔN = N_f − N₀ = 2. Final answer: 2. (c) Accounting for ΔA = 0, charge conservation gives 2 weak beta transitions. Final answer: 2.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Z_final − Z_parent with sign to obtain −2.
Computes N = A − Z for parent and daughter and takes N_final − N_parent.
Evaluates correctly to 2.
Links single-quark flavour conversion to ΔZ = ±1 per weak beta step.
Evaluates correctly to 2.

items.stem: Inside a refractory-foil elastic alpha-scattering chamber, a 5.7 MeV alpha particle (charge +2e) comes momentarily to rest at minimum separation d before reversing direction in front of a tungsten nucleus (Z = 74, A = 184). Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Eₖ = 5.7 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 9.12 × 10⁻¹³ J. d = k(2e)(74e) / Eₖ = 3.73 × 10⁻¹⁴ m = 37.3 fm. Final answer: 37.3 fm. (b) R = 1.20 × (184)^(1/3) = 6.83 fm (< d, confirming pure electrostatic scattering). Final answer: 6.83 fm. (c) ρ = (184 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷) / ((4/3)π(6.83 × 10⁻¹⁵)³) = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. Final answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Converts Eₖ to joules, equates Eₖ = k Q₁ Q₂ / d, and converts metres to femtometres.
Evaluates correctly to 37.3 fm.
Applies R = 1.20 × A^(1/3) fm.
Evaluates correctly to 6.83 fm.
Evaluates ρ = A u / ((4/3)πR³) in SI units.
Evaluates correctly to 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

Evaluates correctly to 6.79 fm.
Multiplies R in fm by 10⁻¹⁵ m fm⁻¹ to obtain 6.79 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.
Divides nuclear mass A u by spherical volume (4/3)πR³.
Evaluates correctly to 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

items.stem: During an optical spectroscopy run on a monochromatic sodium street-lighting discharge cell, sodium vapour atoms populate the first excited state at −3.07 eV, alongside a bound state at −5.23 eV below the zero-eV continuum limit. Constants: h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What minimum photon frequency is required to ionize the atom from the first excited state?
items.workedSolution: Energy needed to reach the continuum is ΔE = 3.07 eV = 4.91 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Threshold frequency f = ΔE / h = 4.91 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 7.41 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f = |E| e / h to obtain 7.41 × 10¹⁴ Hz (B).

items.stem: A radiation detector in a positron-imaging elution calibrator operates in a steady background of 42 counts min⁻¹. A fresh gallium-68 specimen with half-life 68 min gives an initial uncorrected reading of 682 counts min⁻¹. Consider the detector response after 272 min. What total count rate (including background) does the detector record at t = 272 min?
items.workedSolution: Initial net count rate C₀ = 682 − 42 = 640 counts min⁻¹. Number of half-lives n = 272 / 68 = 4. Remaining net count rate C = 640 / 2^4 = 40 counts min⁻¹. Total recorded count rate = 40 + 42 = 82.0 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background (640), divides by 2^4 (40), and adds 42 back to obtain 82.0 counts min⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides the initial total count rate directly by 2ⁿ without subtracting the background count rate first.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Correctly halves the background-subtracted net count rate but forgets to add the background count rate back to obtain the total detector reading.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides the net count rate by 2n instead of 2ⁿ.

items.stem: Quality-assurance logs in a neuroendocrine PET diagnostic unit record an initial population of 1.3 × 10¹⁴ gallium-68 nuclei with half-life 67.7 min. Consider the source after 50.1 min of continuous exponential decay. What is the activity of the sample, in becquerels (Bq), at t = 50.1 min?
items.workedSolution: T₁/₂ = 67.7 × 60 = 4.06 × 10³ s, so λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂ = 1.71 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. Initial activity A₀ = λN₀ = 2.22 × 10¹⁰ Bq. At t = 50.1 min, A = A₀ e^(−λt) = 1.33 × 10¹⁰ Bq.

markScheme.criterion: Converts T₁/₂ to seconds, finds A₀ = λN₀, and evaluates A = A₀ e^(−λt) = 1.33 × 10¹⁰ Bq (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Fails to convert half-life from min to seconds (× 60) when computing A = λN in Bq (s⁻¹).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the initial activity A₀ = λN₀ at t = 0 without multiplying by the exponential decay factor e^(−λt).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses λ = 1 / T₁/₂ instead of λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂ when converting half-life to decay constant.

items.stem: A negative muon decays via the weak interaction: $\mu^- \to e^- + X + \nu_\mu$. Which particle is $X$?
items.workedSolution: $\mu^-$ has $L_\mu = +1, L_e = 0$; $e^-$ has $L_e = +1$ and $\nu_\mu$ has $L_\mu = +1$, so $X$ must carry $L_e = -1$ and $Q = 0$: an electron antineutrino. Therefore option D is correct: electron antineutrino.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: electron antineutrino.

Take $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$, $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, and $m_{\text{e}} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2m_{\text{e}}eV} = 21.7 pm$. (b) Increasing $V$ raises momentum and reduces $\lambda$, so diffraction rings move closer together as de Broglie wavelength decreases.

markScheme.criterion: Equate $eV = \frac{1}{2}m_{\text{e}}v^2$ to find momentum $p = \sqrt{2m_{\text{e}}eV}$.
Substitute into $\lambda = h/p$.
Obtain $\lambda = 21.7 pm$.
Higher anode p.d. increases electron momentum and reduces de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$.
Diffraction rings move closer together (reject particle repulsion).

items.stem: Within a laser-produced ablation plasma plume, one-electron four-times ionized boron B⁴⁺ (Z = 5) ions populate principal shell n = 1 under the Bohr scaling law Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV relative to zero continuum energy (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).
items.workedSolution: (a) Eₙ = −13.6 × (5)² / (1)² = −340 eV. Ionization energy ΔE = 0 − Eₙ = 340 eV. Final answer: 340 eV. (b) ΔE = 340 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 5.44 × 10⁻¹⁷ J. f = ΔE / h = 5.44 × 10⁻¹⁷ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 8.21 × 10¹⁶ Hz. Final answer: 8.21 × 10¹⁶ Hz. (c) λ = (3.00 × 10⁸) / (8.21 × 10¹⁶) = 3.66 nm. Final answer: 3.66 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ΔE = 13.6 Z² / n² eV for the specified Z and n.
Evaluates correctly to 340 eV.
Converts ionization energy from eV to J and divides by Planck's constant h.
Evaluates correctly to 8.21 × 10¹⁶ Hz.

items.workedSolution: (a) Eₖ = qV = 2.00 × 10⁻¹⁶ J. v = √(2Eₖ / m) = 4.89 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Final answer: 4.89 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. (b) λ = h / (mv) = 8.10 × 10⁻¹³ m = 8.10 × 10⁻⁴ nm. Final answer: 8.10 × 10⁻⁴ nm. (c) λ = 0.810 pm. Final answer: 0.810 pm.

items.stem: A bone phantom of density 1800 kg m⁻³ exhibits a linear attenuation coefficient of 54.0 m⁻¹ at 70 kV. What is its mass attenuation coefficient $\mu_m$?
items.workedSolution: Mass attenuation coefficient is $\mu_m = \frac{\mu}{\rho} = \frac{54.0}{1800} = 0.0300 m² kg⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 0.0300 m² kg⁻¹.

items.stem: Energy-balance modelling of a pressurized-water thermal fission reactor fuel pin considers barium–krypton thermal fission of U-235: uranium nucleus (234.99345 u) + 1 thermal neutron (1.008665 u) → barium-141 nucleus (140.88354 u) + krypton-92 nucleus (91.90645 u) + 3 neutrons (each 1.008665 u). Use u = 931.5 MeV c⁻² and elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the rest-mass decrease Δm, in atomic mass units (u), in a single fission reaction?
items.workedSolution: Summing reactant and product rest masses gives Δm = Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 0.186 u.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 0.186 u (B).

items.stem: Electrons are liberated from an alkali-metal sodium photocathode vacuum chamber (work function 2.36 eV) when monochromatic light of frequency 1.29 × 10¹⁵ Hz is incident in vacuum. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Φ = 2.36 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.78 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. f₀ = Φ / h = 3.78 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 5.70 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Final answer: 5.70 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (b) Photon energy E = hf / e = 5.35 eV. Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 5.35 − 2.36 = 2.99 eV. Final answer: 2.99 eV. (c) Vₛ = Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / e = 2.99 V. Final answer: 2.99 V.

markScheme.criterion: Converts Φ from eV to joules and applies f₀ = Φ / h.
Evaluates correctly to 5.70 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
Applies Einstein's photoelectric equation Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = hf/e − Φ.
Evaluates correctly to 2.99 eV.
Uses eVₛ = Eₖ,ₘₐₓ to obtain 2.99 V.

items.stem: Why should the background count in Required Practical 12 be recorded over 15–20 minutes (with the source sealed away in its lead box) rather than for 30 seconds?
items.workedSolution: RP12 mark-scheme precision: Radioactive decay is random so a long counting interval records a much larger total count N, reducing random percentage uncertainty; throughout, handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset.

options.text: Radioactive decay is random so a long counting interval records a much larger total count N, reducing random percentage uncertainty; throughout, handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset.

options.label: B
options.text: Because background radiation decays exponentially during the first 10 minutes of a lesson.
options.distractorRationale: Natural background count rate is approximately constant in mean over a lesson; longer intervals cut random statistical spread √N/N.

options.label: C
options.text: Because a 20-minute background measurement eliminates all statistical randomness in the GM tube.
options.distractorRationale: Long intervals reduce random percentage uncertainty but never eliminate the random nature of decay.

options.label: D
options.text: Because background radiation consists entirely of alpha particles that take 15 minutes to reach the tube.
options.distractorRationale: Background radiation includes cosmic rays, radon, and terrestrial gamma/beta emitters arriving continuously at random times.

items.stem: A singly charged negative chlorine ion $^{35}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ is accelerated in an ion source. Take $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, $m_{\text{p}} = 1.673 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, $m_{\text{n}} = 1.675 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, and $m_{\text{e}} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $N = 35 - 17 = 18$; electrons $= 18$. (b) $m = 5.861 × 10⁻²⁶ kg$, $Q = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C$, so $Q/m = 2.73 × 10⁶ C kg⁻¹$. (c) ion charge equals excess or deficit electrons while total mass includes all nucleons.

markScheme.criterion: Correct neutron number $N = 18$.
Correct orbital electron count $= 18$.
Calculate total mass $m = 5.86 × 10⁻²⁶ kg$ including both protons and neutrons.
Substitute net charge $Q = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C$ into $Q/m$.
Obtain specific charge $= 2.73 × 10⁶ C kg⁻¹$.
State that ion charge equals excess or deficit electrons while total mass includes all nucleons.

items.stem: Spent nuclear fuel rods contain intensely hot, long-lived radioactive fission products (high-level waste). Which sequence describes the safe multi-stage management of high-level radioactive waste?
items.workedSolution: High-level radioactive fission fragments are handled remotely in cooling ponds, vitrified in glass inside steel canisters, and stored in deep geologically stable underground repositories. Therefore the correct statement is: Safe disposal requires that high-level radioactive fission fragments are handled remotely in cooling ponds, vitrified in glass inside steel canisters, and stored in deep geologically stable underground repositories

options.distractorRationale: High-level waste must be strictly contained and isolated from the biosphere.

options.distractorRationale: Chemical reactions cannot alter nuclear decay rates or half-lives.

items.stem: An unstable isotope X lies directly above the stability belt at moderate Z. Which nuclear transition moves X closer to the line of stability?
items.workedSolution: Nuclei above the belt have a high N/Z ratio and undergo beta-minus emission converting a neutron into a proton to lower the high N/Z ratio. Therefore the correct statement is: It undergoes beta-minus emission converting a neutron into a proton to lower the high N/Z ratio

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: beta-minus emission converting a neutron into a proton to lower the high N/Z ratio.

options.label: A
options.text: It undergoes beta-plus emission converting a proton into a neutron to increase the N/Z ratio even further.
options.distractorRationale: Moving further above the belt pushes the nuclide away from stability.

options.label: B
options.text: It undergoes alpha emission even though its proton number is far below eighty-two.
options.distractorRationale: Nuclides above the belt at low/medium Z are neutron-rich and decay via β⁻ rather than α.

options.label: C
options.text: It undergoes electron capture to add another neutron and reduce proton number by one.
options.distractorRationale: Electron capture serves proton-rich nuclei below the belt, not neutron-rich nuclei above it.

options.label: D
options.text: It undergoes beta-minus emission converting a neutron into a proton to lower the high N/Z ratio

items.stem: Nuclear physicists direct a 250 MeV electron beam onto an isotopically pure iron-56 (A = 56) foil. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) λ = 4.97 fm. (b) R = 4.40 fm. (c) ρ = 2.61 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. (d) high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound.

The first non-zero diffraction minimum occurs at θ_min = 43.6°. Using sin θ ≈ 0.61 λ / R, calculate the nuclear radius R of iron-56 in femtometres.
Taking nucleon mass u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, calculate the density of the iron-56 nucleus.
Explain why high-energy electron diffraction determines nuclear radius more accurately than Rutherford alpha closest approach.
parts.expectedAnswer: Electron diffraction is superior because high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound.

items.stem: In Required Practical 12, a student records 420 background counts in 20 minutes before mounting a sealed gamma source opposite a GM tube. At measured ruler separations $x_1 = 160$ mm and $x_2 = 440$ mm, the raw count rates are 116.9 s⁻¹ and 17.71 s⁻¹ respectively.
items.workedSolution: (a) $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 0.350 s⁻¹$. (b) Subtracting background gives $C_{\mathrm{corr},1} = 116.5$ s⁻¹ and $C_{\mathrm{corr},2} = 17.36$ s⁻¹; gradient of $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ vs $x$ is 0.526, so $k = 1/\mathrm{grad}^2 = 3.61 s⁻¹ m²$. (c) $x_0 = 16.0 mm$. (d) handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset.

markScheme.criterion: Background count rate $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 0.350 s⁻¹$.
Subtracts $C_{\mathrm{bg}}$ from both raw rates and calculates $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$.
Finds gradient $\Delta(1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}})/\Delta x = 1/\sqrt{k}$.
Inverse-square constant $k = 3.61 s⁻¹ m²$.
Solves $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}} = (x + x_0)/\sqrt{k}$ (or intercept/gradient) for $x_0$.
Systematic offset $x_0 = 16.0 mm$.
Long tongs + maximise distance + minimise time out of lead-lined box (reject bare 'do not touch').
Explains $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ vs $x$ remains linear despite unknown $x_0$ (whereas $C$ vs $1/x^2$ curves).
Identifies negative x-intercept $-x_0$ as the hidden offset inside source capsule and GM tube.

parts.prompt: Calculate the background count rate $C_{\mathrm{bg}}$ in s⁻¹.
Subtract background radiation, compute $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ at both positions, and determine the inverse-square constant $k$ from the gradient of $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against $x$.
Determine the hidden internal systematic offset $x_0$ in mm.
State the required radiological safety precautions and explain why plotting $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against $x$ is preferred over $C_{\mathrm{corr}}$ against $1/x^2$.
parts.expectedAnswer: handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset
workingSteps: Long tongs, maximum distance, point source away from people, minimal time outside lead-lined box.
1/√C_corr = (x + x₀)/√k stays strictly linear and directly yields x₀ from negative x-intercept.

items.stem: During a Paper 3A planning task, a student notices that plotting corrected gamma count rate against $1/x^2$ gives a curved graph rather than a straight line through the origin.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Before unpacking the sealed source, keep it locked in its lead-lined storage box far away and record background counts over a long period (15–20 minutes) to calculate an accurate mean background rate C_bg = N_bg / t_bg with low random percentage uncertainty. Observe strict radiological safety: handle the source strictly with long tongs, point it away from everyone, maximise distance from the source, and minimise time out of lead storage. Clamp the GM tube coaxially facing the source along a metre ruler. Measure counts at least six separations x (e.g. 0.10 m to 0.50 m), increasing counting duration at larger distances (and taking repeats) so total counts remain high enough to limit statistical percentage uncertainty, while avoiding ultra-close distances where GM dead time saturates counts. Compute corrected count rate C_corr = N/t − C_bg at every distance, then plot 1/√C_corr against x. A straight best-fit line verifies C_corr = k / (x + x₀)², with gradient 1/√k (giving k = 1/gradient²) and negative x-intercept −x₀ revealing the hidden internal distance inside the source holder and GM tube.

markScheme.criterion: States authentic radiological safety controls: long tongs, maximise distance, point away from people, and minimise time out of lead-lined storage box (reject bare 'do not touch').
Measures background count over a long duration (15–20 min) with source away in lead box to reduce random percentage uncertainty in C_bg.
Aligns GM tube and source coaxially along a metre ruler and records counts across >= 6 distances (avoiding GM dead-time saturation close in).
Uses longer counting intervals and/or repeats at larger separations so total counts remain large enough to reduce random percentage uncertainty.
Subtracts background rate to obtain C_corr = N/t − C_bg and plots 1/√C_corr against x (explaining why C_corr vs 1/x² curves due to x₀).
Confirms straight line verifies inverse-square law, extracts k = 1/gradient², and reads hidden systematic offset −x₀ from the negative x-intercept.

parts.prompt: Plan an improved Required Practical 12 procedure using $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against $x$, detailing radiological safety, long background measurement, counting strategy, and how both $k$ and $x_0$ are extracted. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset; record background counts over 15–20 minutes with the source sealed away to obtain C_bg, record counts across >= 6 distances using longer counting times at larger distances so total counts stay large, subtract C_bg to form C_corr, plot 1/√C_corr against x for a straight line of gradient 1/√k, and read −x₀ from the negative x-intercept.
workingSteps: Level 1: Strict radiological safety (long tongs, max distance, point away from people, minimal time outside lead-lined box).

Level 2: Record background over 15–20 min before unpacking source; align GM tube coaxially along metre ruler; record counts across >= 6 distances (longer counting time at large x to keep random % uncertainty small).

Level 3: Subtract C_bg -> C_corr, linearize via 1/√C_corr = (x + x₀)/√k, plot 1/√C_corr vs x, confirm straight line (inverse-square law), extract k = 1/grad² and internal offset x₀ from negative x-intercept.

items.stem: In a pressurised-water reactor (PWR), ordinary water serves simultaneously as both moderator and primary coolant around uranium-235 fuel assemblies surrounded by retractable boron control rods.
items.workedSolution: moderator slows neutrons by elastic collisions, control rods absorb neutrons for criticality, coolant transfers thermal energy, thick concrete shields radiation, and high-level waste moves from cooling ponds to vitrification and deep geological storage. In a PWR, the moderator slows neutrons by elastic collisions, control rods absorb neutrons for criticality, coolant transfers thermal energy, thick concrete shields radiation, and high-level waste moves from cooling ponds to vitrification and deep geological storage. Hydrogen nuclei (protons, A = 1) in water closely match the neutron's mass, transferring a large fraction of kinetic energy per elastic collision to produce thermal neutrons without strongly absorbing them, while water's high specific heat capacity transfers core thermal energy efficiently to the steam generator. Boron control rods absorb excess neutrons to keep k = 1 (or drop fully under gravity for emergency shutdown), while the thick steel pressure vessel and dense concrete biological shield absorb penetrating γ rays and escaping neutrons. High-level spent fuel containing intense β⁻/γ-emitting fission fragments is moved by remote manipulators into water-filled cooling ponds for several years, then vitrified inside borosilicate glass sealed in stainless-steel canisters for deep geologically stable underground storage.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: Explains water slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds via elastic collisions with low-mass hydrogen nuclei (close mass match maximises KE transfer; reject 'moderator absorbs').
L1b: Notes thermal neutrons have a much higher probability of inducing U-235 fission, and water also carries thermal energy to the heat exchanger/steam generator.
L2a: Explains boron control rods absorb neutrons to maintain critical operation (one fission neutron causing one subsequent fission) or shut the reactor down.
L2b: States thick steel pressure vessel and thick concrete biological shield attenuate intense gamma radiation and stray neutrons.
L3a: Explains spent fuel high-level waste is handled remotely and stored in cooling ponds for thermal dissipation of decay heat and radiation shielding.
L3b: Explains long-term immobilisation via vitrification in glass sealed in stainless-steel canisters stored in deep geologically stable underground repositories.

items.stem: Unstable nuclides occur in three distinct zones around the N–Z stability belt: very heavy isotopes (Z > 82), neutron-rich isotopes above the belt, and proton-rich medical isotopes below the belt.
items.workedSolution: above proton number twenty, long-range electrostatic repulsion between all protons grows faster than short-range strong nuclear attraction requiring a higher N/Z ratio. Because the strong nuclear force only acts between neighbouring nucleons (attractive to ~3 fm, repulsive below ~0.5 fm), above proton number twenty, long-range electrostatic repulsion between all protons grows faster than short-range strong nuclear attraction requiring a higher N/Z ratio; thus heavy elements cannot be stable on N = Z. Heavy nuclei above Z = 82 undergo α decay (ΔZ = −2, ΔN = −2). Neutron-rich nuclei above the belt have a high N/Z ratio and undergo β⁻ decay (n → p + e⁻ + ν̄_e; ΔZ = +1, ΔN = −1), while proton-rich nuclei below the belt undergo β⁺ decay or electron capture (p → n + e⁺ + ν_e; ΔZ = −1, ΔN = +1). Reactor fission products inherit the high N/Z ratio of uranium-235, placing them well above the medium-Z stability belt, so they emit intense β⁻ particles and accompanying de-excitation γ rays.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: Specifies strong nuclear force range (attractive up to ~3 fm, repulsive below ~0.5 fm) vs long-range electrostatic repulsion between all protons.
L1b: Explains heavy nuclei require a higher N/Z ratio (bending above N = Z for Z > 20) because extra neutrons add strong attraction without electrostatic repulsion.
L2a: Gives α decay for Z > 82 with ΔZ = −2 and ΔN = −2.
L2b: Gives β⁻ decay (explicit minus sign) above the belt: neutron converts to proton (ΔZ = +1, ΔN = −1), lowering N/Z.
L3a: Gives β⁺ / electron capture below the belt: proton converts to neutron (ΔZ = −1, ΔN = +1), raising N/Z.
L3b: Explains reactor fission products are neutron-rich with a high N/Z ratio above the stability belt, emitting intense β⁻ radiation (and γ photons from excited daughters).

parts.prompt: Explain why no completely stable nuclei exist along N = Z for heavy elements, describe the exact N–Z vector shift and nucleon transformation for α, β⁻, and β⁺ decay, and explain why fission products from nuclear reactors require heavy beta-gamma shielding.
parts.expectedAnswer: above proton number twenty, long-range electrostatic repulsion between all protons grows faster than short-range strong nuclear attraction requiring a higher N/Z ratio. Because the strong nuclear force only acts between neighbouring nucleons (attractive to ~3 fm, repulsive below ~0.5 fm), above proton number twenty, long-range electrostatic repulsion between all protons grows faster than short-range strong nuclear attraction requiring a higher N/Z ratio; thus heavy elements cannot be stable on N = Z. Heavy nuclei above Z = 82 undergo α decay (ΔZ = −2, ΔN = −2). Neutron-rich nuclei above the belt have a high N/Z ratio and undergo β⁻ decay (n → p + e⁻ + ν̄_e; ΔZ = +1, ΔN = −1), while proton-rich nuclei below the belt undergo β⁺ decay or electron capture (p → n + e⁺ + ν_e; ΔZ = −1, ΔN = +1). Reactor fission products inherit the high N/Z ratio of uranium-235, placing them well above the medium-Z stability belt, so they emit intense β⁻ particles and accompanying de-excitation γ rays.
workingSteps: Contrast strong nuclear force range (< 3 fm, repulsive < 0.5 fm) with long-range electrostatic repulsion among all protons.
Specify exact ΔZ, ΔN shifts and nucleon conversions for α, β⁻, and β⁺/EC.
Connect high N/Z ratio of fission products to intense β⁻ and γ emission.

items.stem: Physicists scatter a monoenergetic beam of 250 MeV electrons off thin foils of carbon-12, iron-56, and lead-208 to investigate how nuclear size and density vary across the periodic table.
items.workedSolution: high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound. Electrons at 250 MeV have relativistic de Broglie wavelength λ ≈ hc/E ~ 5 fm (comparable to nuclear diameter), enabling measurable diffraction; crucially, high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound distorted by strong-force interaction and recoil. From sin θ ≈ 0.61λ/R, as target nucleon number increases from A = 12 to A = 208, nuclear radius R = R₀ A^(1/3) grows larger, so the non-zero first diffraction minimum shifts to a smaller scattering angle θ_min. Confirming a straight line through the origin for R³ versus A (or lg R vs lg A of gradient 1/3) proves nuclear volume is proportional to A, yielding constant density ρ = 3u / (4πR₀³) independent of A.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: Explains 250 MeV gives electron de Broglie wavelength λ ~ 10⁻¹⁵ m comparable to nuclear dimensions for observable diffraction.
L1b: Contrasts leptonic electrons (no strong nuclear interaction, direct R measurement) against alpha particles (hadronic strong force, energy-dependent upper bound only).
L2a: Identifies the non-zero first diffraction minimum obeying sin θ ≈ 0.61 λ / R.
L2b: Deduces that larger A (Pb-208 vs C-12) gives larger R = R₀ A^(1/3), shifting the first minimum to a smaller angle θ_min.
L3a: Explains how plotting R against A^(1/3) (or R³ vs A) yields a straight line through the origin confirming V ∝ A.
L3b: Proves nuclear density ρ = 3u / (4πR₀³) is independent of A, implying nucleons are packed tightly at uniform density across all nuclei.

options.text: The strong nuclear force is always attractive down to zero separation and falls as inverse distance squared to infinity.
options.distractorRationale: Without short-range repulsion (< 0.5 fm) nuclei would collapse to a point, and strong force vanishes beyond ~3 fm.

options.label: B
options.text: The strong nuclear force is attractive up to about three femtometres and becomes strongly repulsive below half a femtometre

options.label: C
options.text: The strong nuclear force is repulsive above three femtometres and attractive only between protons.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses sign with range and forgets that the strong force acts equally on protons and neutrons.

options.label: D
options.text: The strong nuclear force acts over atomic radii of order ten to the minus ten metres to bind orbital electrons.
options.distractorRationale: Electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force.

items.stem: Cosmic-ray muons created high in the atmosphere reach sea-level detectors in large numbers despite a very short rest lifetime of 2.2 μs. How is this observation reconciled consistently in both the Earth reference frame and the muon's own rest frame?
items.workedSolution: Relativity resolves the muon paradox consistently: in Earth frame muon lifetime is time dilated whereas in the muon rest frame atmosphere depth is length contracted.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that in Earth frame muon lifetime is time dilated whereas in the muon rest frame atmosphere depth is length contracted.

options.label: A
options.text: In Earth frame atmosphere depth is length contracted whereas in the muon rest frame muon lifetime is dilated.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses which frame observes proper length vs proper time.

options.label: B
options.text: Muons exceed the speed of light in the upper atmosphere before slowing near sea level.
options.distractorRationale: No massive particle can reach or exceed c.

options.label: C
options.text: Both frames agree because in Earth frame muon lifetime is time dilated whereas in the muon rest frame atmosphere depth is length contracted.

options.label: D
options.text: Both time dilation and length contraction simultaneously double the muon's survival probability in Earth frame.
options.distractorRationale: You apply time dilation in Earth's frame OR length contraction in the muon's frame—never both to the same frame.

items.stem: Coincidence spectroscopy in a Type Ia supernova light-curve nickel-cobalt-iron chain observes nickel (A = 56, Z = 28) decaying via purely weak beta-plus transitions (u → d + e⁺ + νₑ) into a product state at A = 56 and Z = 26. How many individual quark-level u → d weak beta transitions occur between the parent and final nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Each weak beta step flips exactly one quark inside a nucleon, changing Z by −1 while keeping A constant. Accounting for ΔA = 0 gives 2 weak quark transitions.

markScheme.criterion: Balances A and Z to identify 2 single-quark weak beta transitions (B).

items.stem: A collimated proton (charge +1e) carrying 5.7 MeV of kinetic energy undergoes direct head-on Coulomb backscattering from a stationary silver nucleus (Z = 47, A = 107) inside a silicon-diode nuclear recoil goniometer. Constants: k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the distance of closest approach d, in femtometres (fm)?
items.workedSolution: Initial kinetic energy Eₖ = 5.7 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 9.12 × 10⁻¹³ J. At the turning point, Eₖ = k(1e)(47e) / d, so d = (8.99 × 10⁹)(1)(47)(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)² / 9.12 × 10⁻¹³ = 11.9 fm.

markScheme.criterion: Equates Eₖ to k Q₁ Q₂ / d to obtain d = 11.9 fm (B).

items.stem: Radiochemical assay of a monazite mineral sand deposit tracks a thorium parent nuclide (A = 232, Z = 90) through sequential alpha and beta-minus decays into a daughter nuclide having A = 212 and Z = 82. How many beta-minus particles are emitted in this decay sequence?
items.workedSolution: Only alpha decay changes nucleon number A: Nα = (232 − 212) / 4 = 5. Proton balance gives 82 = 90 − 2(5) + Nβ⁻, so Nβ⁻ = 82 − 80 = 2.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Nα = 5 from ΔA / 4 and solves Z_f = Z_0 − 2Nα + Nβ⁻ to obtain Nβ⁻ = 2 (A).

items.stem: Monochromatic radiation of frequency $980\text{ THz}$ illuminates a potassium surface of work function $2.30\text{ eV}$. Using $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$ and $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, calculate the stopping potential $V_{\text{s}}$.
items.workedSolution: Photon energy $E = hf/e = (6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 980 \times 10^{12}) / 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 4.06 eV$, so $V_{\text{s}} = (hf - \phi)/e = 1.76 V$. Option D (1.76 V) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Stopping potential $V_{\text{s}} = 1.76 V$ (1.76 V, option D).

items.stem: To verify wave-particle duality, a 390 V electron beam is directed perpendicularly onto polycrystalline graphite (110) planes (d = 1.23 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) at distance L = 0.13 m from a detector screen. Take first-order ring geometry sin θ = λ / d and r = L tan θ, with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the first-order diffraction angle θ, in degrees?
items.workedSolution: Electron wavelength λ = h / √(2mₑeV) = 6.22 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Using sin θ = λ / d = 0.506 yields θ = arcsin(0.506) = 30.4 °.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates λ = h / √(2mₑeV) and θ = arcsin(λ / d) = 30.4 ° (C).

items.stem: A vapour cell in a cold-cathode neon spectroscopy tube contains neon gas whose the second excited state lies at −3.04 eV and whose adjacent bound level lies at −4.86 eV relative to the continuum threshold. Assume h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) ΔE = 0 − (−3.04) = 3.04 eV. Final answer: 3.04 eV. (b) ΔE = 3.04 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.86 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. f = ΔE / h = 4.86 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 7.34 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Final answer: 7.34 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (c) λ = c / f = (3.00 × 10⁸) / (7.34 × 10¹⁴) = 4.09 × 10⁻⁷ m. Converting to nanometres gives λ = 409 nm. Final answer: 409 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds ΔE = 0 − E_initial in eV to obtain 3.04 eV.
Converts ΔE to joules (× 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) and applies f = ΔE / h.
Evaluates correctly to 7.34 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
Uses λ = c / f (or hc / ΔE) and converts metres to nanometres.
Evaluates correctly to 409 nm.

Calculate the new de Broglie wavelength when the anode potential difference is raised to 112.5 kV.
Explain why raising the anode voltage improves image detail, and state two practical factors that still limit TEM resolution.
parts.expectedAnswer: Higher voltage reduces de Broglie wavelength and diffraction blurring; however, sample thickness slows electrons increasing wavelength and magnetic lens aberrations with spread of speeds blur the image.
workingSteps: Shorter $\lambda$ reduces diffraction limits, improving potential resolution.
Thick samples slow electrons (increasing $\lambda$) and magnetic lens aberrations / speed spread blur focus.

items.stem: Before testing an iodine-123 sample (half-life 13.2 h) in a gamma-camera collimator test rig, ambient background radiation registers 22 counts min⁻¹. Introducing the source raises the total detector reading to 1462 counts min⁻¹ initially, and monitoring continues for an elapsed interval of 66 h.
items.workedSolution: (a) C₀,net = 1462 − 22 = 1.44 × 10³ counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 1.44 × 10³ counts min⁻¹. (b) n = 66 / 13.2 = 5 half-lives. C_net = 1440 / 2^5 = 45.0 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 45.0 counts min⁻¹. (c) C_total = 45 + 22 = 67.0 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 67.0 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background count rate from initial total count rate to obtain 1.44 × 10³ counts min⁻¹.
Identifies 5 elapsed half-lives and divides initial net count rate by 2^5.
Evaluates correctly to 45.0 counts min⁻¹.
Adds background count rate back to the remaining net count rate to obtain 67.0 counts min⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Determine the initial corrected count rate due solely to the iodine-123 source at t = 0.
Calculate the corrected count rate from the source alone at t = 66 h.
State the total count rate displayed by the detector at t = 66 h.

items.stem: Quality-assurance logs in a cyclotron radiochemistry laboratory record an initial population of 5.8 × 10¹³ copper-64 nuclei with half-life 12.7 h. Consider the source after 27.7 h of continuous exponential decay.

markScheme.criterion: Converts T₁/₂ from h to seconds and applies λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂.
Evaluates correctly to 1.52 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.
Multiplies λ in s⁻¹ by N₀ using A₀ = λN₀.
Evaluates correctly to 8.79 × 10⁸ Bq.
Applies exponential decay law A = A₀ e^(−λt) with consistent time units.
Evaluates correctly to 1.94 × 10⁸ Bq.

parts.prompt: Show the conversion of the half-life to seconds and calculate the decay constant λ in s⁻¹.
Calculate the initial activity A₀ of the sample, in Bq, at t = 0.
Determine the activity A of the sample, in Bq, after t = 27.7 h.

Correctly evaluate lepton numbers / strangeness S on both sides.
State neutral kaon.
State d s-bar.
Explicitly link strangeness conservation (ΔS = 0 strong) vs strangeness change (ΔS = 0, ±1 weak).

items.stem: Why does a low-pressure mercury discharge lamp emit light at specific discrete wavelengths rather than a continuous spectrum before hitting the phosphor wall?
items.workedSolution: Atomic energy levels are discrete, so de-excitation transitions emit photons of exact energies $hf = E_1 - E_2$. Therefore option B is correct: colliding free electrons excite mercury orbital electrons emitting ultraviolet photons absorbed by phosphor coating.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: colliding free electrons excite mercury orbital electrons emitting ultraviolet photons absorbed by phosphor coating.

options.text: Discrete spectral lines occur because mercury atoms can absorb and emit any continuous amount of energy
options.distractorRationale: Continuous energy levels would produce a continuous spectrum, not sharp lines.

options.label: B
options.text: Discrete spectral lines occur because colliding free electrons excite mercury orbital electrons emitting ultraviolet photons absorbed by phosphor coating between quantised energy levels so only specific photon energies hf occur

options.label: C
options.text: Discrete spectral lines occur because glass absorbs all frequencies except one single colour
options.distractorRationale: Line spectra are a property of quantised atomic energy levels inside the gas.

options.label: D
options.text: Discrete spectral lines occur because all free electrons have identical kinetic energy after colliding
options.distractorRationale: Colliding electrons transfer discrete ΔE and carry away any leftover kinetic energy.

Evaluates correctly to −0.989.

items.stem: Observations of a solar prominence EUV grating spectrometer detect continuum photoionization edges from hydrogenic helium He⁺ (Z = 2) in excited shell n = 4, where discrete levels satisfy Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV. Constants: h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What minimum photon frequency is needed to remove the electron completely from excited shell n = 4?
items.workedSolution: Ionization energy from n = 4 is ΔE = 13.6 × 2² / 4² = 3.40 eV = 5.44 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Threshold frequency f = ΔE / h = 8.21 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates f = (13.6 Z² / n²)(e / h) = 8.21 × 10¹⁴ Hz (C).

items.stem: Nuclear mass tables from an iron-peak maximum-stability mass trap list a stripped nickel-62 nucleus (A = 62, Z = 28) at rest mass 61.912927 u. Assume mₚ = 1.007276 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u, and u = 931.5 MeV c⁻². What is the binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, of this nickel-62 nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Neutron count N = 62 − 28 = 34. Mass defect Δm = 28(1.007276) + 34(1.008665) − 61.912927 = 0.585 u. Total binding energy B = Δm × 931.5 = 545 MeV. Binding energy per nucleon B / A = 545 / 62 = 8.80 MeV.

markScheme.criterion: Computes Δm = 0.585 u, B = 545 MeV, and B / A = 8.80 MeV (A).

items.stem: A collimated beam of thermal neutrons emerges from a heavy-water research-reactor velocity selector at speed 2200 m s⁻¹. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and mₙ = 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. What is the de Broglie wavelength, in nanometres (nm), of the thermal neutrons?
items.workedSolution: Momentum p = mv = (1.67 × 10⁻²⁷)(2200) = 3.69 × 10⁻²⁴ N s. De Broglie wavelength λ = h / p = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (3.69 × 10⁻²⁴) = 0.180 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates p and λ = h / p to obtain 0.180 nm (D).

items.workedSolution: (a) $\lambda_{\min} = 13.1 pm$. (b) $x_{1/2} = 14.4 mm$. (c) aluminium filter absorbs low energy soft X-rays that would raise patient skin dose without reaching the detector.

items.stem: A nuclear data benchmark for a laser-driven proton–boron aneutronic fusion experiment specifies proton (1.007276 u) + boron-11 nucleus (11.006562 u) → 3 alpha particles (each of mass 4.001506 u) (with mass-energy equivalent u = 931.5 MeV c⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).
items.workedSolution: (a) Δm = Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 9.32 × 10⁻³ u. Final answer: 9.32 × 10⁻³ u. (b) Q = 9.32 × 10⁻³ × 931.5 = 8.68 MeV. Final answer: 8.68 MeV. (c) Total nucleon number A = 12. Final answer: 12.

markScheme.criterion: Sums all reactant and product rest masses including particle multiplicities.
Evaluates correctly to 9.32 × 10⁻³ u.
Multiplies Δm in u by 931.5 MeV u⁻¹.
Evaluates correctly to 8.68 MeV.
Sums nucleon numbers across reactants (or products) to obtain 12.

items.stem: Electrons are liberated from a high-vacuum tungsten filament surface (work function 4.55 eV) when monochromatic light of frequency 2.48 × 10¹⁵ Hz is incident in vacuum. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What reverse stopping potential Vₛ is required to reduce the collector photocurrent to zero?
items.workedSolution: Photon energy E = hf / e = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 2.48 × 10¹⁵) / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 10.3 eV. Maximum kinetic energy Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = E − Φ = 10.3 − 4.55 = 5.73 eV. Hence stopping potential Vₛ = 5.73 V.

markScheme.criterion: Computes eVₛ = hf − Φ to obtain Vₛ = 5.73 V (A).

items.stem: Along an evacuated drift-tube section of rest-frame length L₀ = 22.3 m in the laboratory hall, charged pions in a linear accelerator coast at uniform velocity v = 0.8c with pion rest-frame proper lifetime Δt₀ = 3.22 × 10⁻⁸ s. What contracted length L of the baseline L₀ is measured in the moving rest frame?
items.workedSolution: Lorentz factor γ = 1 / √(1 − 0.8²) = 1.67. Contracted length L = L₀ / γ = 22.3 / 1.67 = 13.4 m.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates γ = 1.67 and L = L₀ / γ = 13.4 m (D).

items.stem: In an ultra-high-vacuum time-of-flight spectrometer, monochromatic UV light of wavelength 142 nm strikes a clean tungsten sample of work function 4.55 eV. markScheme.criterion: Evaluates λ₀ = hc / Φ = 273 nm (A).

items.stem: A proton and antiproton collide with combined kinetic energy $120\text{ MeV}$ and annihilate into two gamma photons of equal energy. Rest energy of a proton $= 938.257\text{ MeV}$, $1\text{ MeV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$, $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Each photon has $E = 998 MeV$, giving $f = 2.41 × 10²³ Hz$. (b) two gamma photons travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum.

markScheme.criterion: Each photon energy $= 998 MeV$.
Convert photon energy to joules and apply $f = E/h$.
Frequency $= 2.41 × 10²³ Hz$.
Momentum must be conserved (initial momentum ~ 0).
Two gamma photons travel in opposite directions with equal magnitude momentum.

parts.prompt: Calculate the energy of each emitted gamma photon in MeV and its frequency in Hz.
parts.expectedAnswer: Each photon energy $= 998 MeV$; frequency $= 2.41 × 10²³ Hz$
workingSteps: Energy of each photon $E = E_0 + \frac{1}{2}E_{\text{k,tot}} = 998 MeV$.
Convert to joules and compute $f = E/h = 2.41 × 10²³ Hz$.

parts.prompt: Explain why two photons are emitted in opposite directions during annihilation.
parts.expectedAnswer: Initial momentum is approximately zero, so two gamma photons travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum.
workingSteps: State momentum conservation from near-zero initial momentum.
Conclude two identical photons travel in opposite directions (reject 'elimination').

items.stem: In Required Practical 12, a student records 450 background counts in 15 minutes before mounting a sealed gamma source opposite a GM tube. At measured ruler separations $x_1 = 110$ mm and $x_2 = 390$ mm, the raw count rates are 100.5 s⁻¹ and 11.61 s⁻¹ respectively.
items.workedSolution: (a) $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 0.500 s⁻¹$. (b) Subtracting background gives $C_{\mathrm{corr},1} = 100.0$ s⁻¹ and $C_{\mathrm{corr},2} = 11.11$ s⁻¹; gradient of $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ vs $x$ is 0.714, so $k = 1/\mathrm{grad}^2 = 1.96 s⁻¹ m²$. (c) $x_0 = 30.0 mm$. (d) handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset.

markScheme.criterion: Background count rate $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 0.500 s⁻¹$.
Subtracts $C_{\mathrm{bg}}$ from both raw rates and calculates $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$.
Finds gradient $\Delta(1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}})/\Delta x = 1/\sqrt{k}$.
Inverse-square constant $k = 1.96 s⁻¹ m²$.
Solves $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}} = (x + x_0)/\sqrt{k}$ (or intercept/gradient) for $x_0$.
Systematic offset $x_0 = 30.0 mm$.
Long tongs + maximise distance + minimise time out of lead-lined box (reject bare 'do not touch').
Explains $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ vs $x$ remains linear despite unknown $x_0$ (whereas $C$ vs $1/x^2$ curves).
Identifies negative x-intercept $-x_0$ as the hidden offset inside source capsule and GM tube.

parts.expectedAnswer: handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset

items.stem: An unstable carbon nucleus undergoes $\beta^-$ decay to form a nitrogen nucleus. How does the specific charge of the nucleus change during this decay?
items.workedSolution: In $\beta^-$ decay, $Z \to Z + 1$ while $A$ is unchanged, so $Q/m$ rises: specific charge increases. Therefore option A is correct: specific charge increases.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: specific charge increases.

items.stem: How does the density of a carbon-12 nucleus compare with the density of a gold-197 nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Since R = R₀ A^(1/3), nuclear volume is proportional to nucleon number so nuclear density is constant and independent of mass number. Therefore the correct statement is: They are essentially identical because nuclear volume is proportional to nucleon number so nuclear density is constant and independent of mass number

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: nuclear volume is proportional to nucleon number so nuclear density is constant and independent of mass number.

options.text: Gold-197 is about sixteen times denser because it packs sixteen times as many nucleons into the same volume.

options.label: B
options.text: Carbon-12 is denser because light nuclei contain no neutrons to dilute proton mass.
options.distractorRationale: Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons, and neutron and proton masses are nearly equal.

options.label: C

items.workedSolution: The moderator slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds via elastic collisions with low-mass nuclei so uranium-235 fission probability increases. options.text: The moderator absorbs excess fast neutrons to shut down the chain reaction safely.
options.distractorRationale: Major AQA mark-scheme trap: control rods absorb neutrons, whereas the moderator must NOT absorb neutrons!

options.label: B
options.text: The moderator slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds via elastic collisions with low-mass nuclei so uranium-235 fission probability increases

options.label: C
options.text: The moderator accelerates slow neutrons to relativistic speeds so they split uranium-238 nuclei.
options.distractorRationale: Thermal reactors require slowing fast fission neutrons down to thermal speeds for U-235.

options.label: D
options.text: The moderator uses heavy lead nuclei so neutrons bounce off elastically with maximum kinetic energy loss.
options.distractorRationale: Elastic collision energy transfer is maximal when moderator nucleon mass is close to neutron mass (low A), not heavy lead.

items.stem: Very heavy nuclei with proton number Z > 82 are too massive for the short-range strong force to hold stably together. Which decay mode moves such a nucleus diagonally down and left on the N–Z chart?
items.workedSolution: Heavy nuclei above Z = 82 undergo alpha emission reducing both proton number and neutron number by two. Therefore the correct statement is: Heavy nuclei undergo alpha emission reducing both proton number and neutron number by two

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: alpha emission reducing both proton number and neutron number by two.

items.stem: An electron spectrometer records the scattered intensity distribution of 350 MeV electrons diffracted by aluminium-27 (A = 27) nuclei. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) λ = 3.55 fm. (b) R = 3.30 fm. (c) ρ = 2.98 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. (d) high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound.

markScheme.criterion: Converts MeV into joules and applies λ = hc / E.
Obtains λ = 3.55 fm.
Rearranges sin θ ≈ 0.61 λ / R for R.
Calculates R = 3.30 fm.
Computes nuclear density ρ = 2.98 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.
States electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and give direct radius via diffraction minimum.

Contrasts with alpha closest approach giving only an energy-dependent upper bound (high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound).

parts.expectedAnswer: Electron diffraction is superior because high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound.

items.stem: In Required Practical 12, a student records 480 background counts in 20 minutes before mounting a sealed gamma source opposite a GM tube. At measured ruler separations $x_1 = 140$ mm and $x_2 = 420$ mm, the raw count rates are 123.9 s⁻¹ and 16.98 s⁻¹ respectively.
items.workedSolution: (a) $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 0.400 s⁻¹$. (b) Subtracting background gives $C_{\mathrm{corr},1} = 123.5$ s⁻¹ and $C_{\mathrm{corr},2} = 16.58$ s⁻¹; gradient of $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ vs $x$ is 0.556, so $k = 1/\mathrm{grad}^2 = 3.24 s⁻¹ m²$. (c) $x_0 = 22.0 mm$. (d) handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset.

markScheme.criterion: Background count rate $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 0.400 s⁻¹$.
Subtracts $C_{\mathrm{bg}}$ from both raw rates and calculates $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$.
Finds gradient $\Delta(1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}})/\Delta x = 1/\sqrt{k}$.
Inverse-square constant $k = 3.24 s⁻¹ m²$.
Solves $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}} = (x + x_0)/\sqrt{k}$ (or intercept/gradient) for $x_0$.
Systematic offset $x_0 = 22.0 mm$.
Long tongs + maximise distance + minimise time out of lead-lined box (reject bare 'do not touch').
Explains $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ vs $x$ remains linear despite unknown $x_0$ (whereas $C$ vs $1/x^2$ curves).
Identifies negative x-intercept $-x_0$ as the hidden offset inside source capsule and GM tube.

Subtract background radiation, compute $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ at both positions, and determine the inverse-square constant $k$ from the gradient of $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against $x$.
Determine the hidden internal systematic offset $x_0$ in mm.
State the required radiological safety precautions and explain why plotting $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against $x$ is preferred over $C_{\mathrm{corr}}$ against $1/x^2$.
parts.expectedAnswer: handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset
workingSteps: Long tongs, maximum distance, point source away from people, minimal time outside lead-lined box.
1/√C_corr = (x + x₀)/√k stays strictly linear and directly yields x₀ from negative x-intercept.

items.stem: A Year 13 student must experimentally verify the inverse-square law for gamma radiation using a sealed cobalt-60 source, a GM tube with counter-timer, and a metre ruler.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Before unpacking the sealed source, keep it locked in its lead-lined storage box far away and record background counts over a long period (15–20 minutes) to calculate an accurate mean background rate C_bg = N_bg / t_bg with low random percentage uncertainty. Observe strict radiological safety: handle the source strictly with long tongs, point it away from everyone, maximise distance from the source, and minimise time out of lead storage. Clamp the GM tube coaxially facing the source along a metre ruler. Measure counts at least six separations x (e.g. 0.10 m to 0.50 m), increasing counting duration at larger distances (and taking repeats) so total counts remain high enough to limit statistical percentage uncertainty, while avoiding ultra-close distances where GM dead time saturates counts. Compute corrected count rate C_corr = N/t − C_bg at every distance, then plot 1/√C_corr against x. A straight best-fit line verifies C_corr = k / (x + x₀)², with gradient 1/√k (giving k = 1/gradient²) and negative x-intercept −x₀ revealing the hidden internal distance inside the source holder and GM tube.

markScheme.criterion: States authentic radiological safety controls: long tongs, maximise distance, point away from people, and minimise time out of lead-lined storage box (reject bare 'do not touch').
Measures background count over a long duration (15–20 min) with source away in lead box to reduce random percentage uncertainty in C_bg.
Aligns GM tube and source coaxially along a metre ruler and records counts across >= 6 distances (avoiding GM dead-time saturation close in).
Uses longer counting intervals and/or repeats at larger separations so total counts remain large enough to reduce random percentage uncertainty.
Subtracts background rate to obtain C_corr = N/t − C_bg and plots 1/√C_corr against x (explaining why C_corr vs 1/x² curves due to x₀).
Confirms straight line verifies inverse-square law, extracts k = 1/gradient², and reads hidden systematic offset −x₀ from the negative x-intercept.

parts.prompt: Describe a safe, high-precision practical procedure to verify the inverse-square law graphically and account for both background radiation and the unknown internal offset $x_0$. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset; record background counts over 15–20 minutes with the source sealed away to obtain C_bg, record counts across >= 6 distances using longer counting times at larger distances so total counts stay large, subtract C_bg to form C_corr, plot 1/√C_corr against x for a straight line of gradient 1/√k, and read −x₀ from the negative x-intercept.
workingSteps: Level 1: Strict radiological safety (long tongs, max distance, point away from people, minimal time outside lead-lined box).

Level 2: Record background over 15–20 min before unpacking source; align GM tube coaxially along metre ruler; record counts across >= 6 distances (longer counting time at large x to keep random % uncertainty small).

Level 3: Subtract C_bg -> C_corr, linearize via 1/√C_corr = (x + x₀)/√k, plot 1/√C_corr vs x, confirm straight line (inverse-square law), extract k = 1/grad² and internal offset x₀ from negative x-intercept.

items.stem: The cutaway schematic shows a thermal nuclear fission reactor using enriched uranium-235 fuel rods, a graphite moderator, boron control rods, pressurised coolant, and a concrete biological shield.
items.workedSolution: moderator slows neutrons by elastic collisions, control rods absorb neutrons for criticality, coolant transfers thermal energy, thick concrete shields radiation, and high-level waste moves from cooling ponds to vitrification and deep geological storage. In a thermal reactor, the moderator slows neutrons by elastic collisions, control rods absorb neutrons for criticality, coolant transfers thermal energy, thick concrete shields radiation, and high-level waste moves from cooling ponds to vitrification and deep geological storage. Specifically: fast fission neutrons collide elastically with low-mass moderator nuclei (graphite or water, which must not absorb neutrons) transferring maximum kinetic energy per collision to reach thermal speeds where U-235 fission cross-section is high. Retractable boron or cadmium control rods absorb neutrons to maintain a critical chain reaction (k = 1, one neutron per fission causing the next). Coolant circulates thermal energy from the core to a heat exchanger/steam generator, while a thick steel pressure vessel and dense concrete biological shield attenuate γ rays and stray neutrons. Intensely hot, radioactive high-level fission-fragment waste is handled remotely, stored in deep cooling ponds for thermal cooling and radiation shielding, vitrified in solid glass inside stainless-steel canisters, and emplaced in deep geologically stable underground storage.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: States moderator (graphite/water) slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds via elastic collisions so U-235 fission probability is high (reject 'absorbs neutrons' for moderator).
L1b: Explains low-nucleon-number moderator atoms transfer more kinetic energy per elastic collision.
L2a: States boron/cadmium control rods absorb neutrons (reject bare 'stop') to regulate a steady critical chain reaction (1 neutron per fission causing next fission).
L2b: States coolant transfers thermal energy to steam generator/heat exchanger AND steel vessel plus thick concrete biological shield absorb γ/neutron radiation.
L3a: Describes high-level waste (fission fragments) handled remotely and placed in cooling ponds to remove decay heat and provide radiation shielding.
L3b: States waste is vitrified in glass inside stainless-steel canisters and placed in deep geologically stable underground storage (reject bare 'bury underground').

parts.prompt: Explain the physical role of the moderator, control rods, coolant, and shielding during steady power generation, and describe the complete safety procedure for handling and disposing of high-level spent fuel waste.
parts.expectedAnswer: moderator slows neutrons by elastic collisions, control rods absorb neutrons for criticality, coolant transfers thermal energy, thick concrete shields radiation, and high-level waste moves from cooling ponds to vitrification and deep geological storage. In a thermal reactor, the moderator slows neutrons by elastic collisions, control rods absorb neutrons for criticality, coolant transfers thermal energy, thick concrete shields radiation, and high-level waste moves from cooling ponds to vitrification and deep geological storage. Specifically: fast fission neutrons collide elastically with low-mass moderator nuclei (graphite or water, which must not absorb neutrons) transferring maximum kinetic energy per collision to reach thermal speeds where U-235 fission cross-section is high. Retractable boron or cadmium control rods absorb neutrons to maintain a critical chain reaction (k = 1, one neutron per fission causing the next). Coolant circulates thermal energy from the core to a heat exchanger/steam generator, while a thick steel pressure vessel and dense concrete biological shield attenuate γ rays and stray neutrons. Intensely hot, radioactive high-level fission-fragment waste is handled remotely, stored in deep cooling ponds for thermal cooling and radiation shielding, vitrified in solid glass inside stainless-steel canisters, and emplaced in deep geologically stable underground storage.
workingSteps: L1: Moderator (graphite/water, low nucleon mass, non-absorbing) slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds via elastic collisions for U-235.
L2: Boron/cadmium control rods absorb neutrons for criticality (k = 1); coolant extracts heat; steel vessel + thick concrete shield radiation.
L3: High-level waste: remote handling → cooling ponds (cooling + shielding) → vitrification in glass/steel canisters → deep geologically stable underground repository.

items.stem: The chart plots neutron number N against proton number Z for stable nuclides alongside the dashed line N = Z and decay regions.
items.workedSolution: above proton number twenty, long-range electrostatic repulsion between all protons grows faster than short-range strong nuclear attraction requiring a higher N/Z ratio. Up to Z ≈ 20, stable nuclei lie along N = Z because each nucleon interacts attractively via the short-range strong nuclear force (attractive up to ~3 fm, strongly repulsive below ~0.5 fm). Above proton number twenty, long-range electrostatic repulsion between all protons grows faster than short-range strong nuclear attraction requiring a higher N/Z ratio, so the stability belt curves upward toward N/Z ≈ 1.5 at Z = 82. Very heavy nuclei (Z > 82) emit α particles (ΔZ = −2, ΔN = −2); neutron-rich nuclei above the belt have a high N/Z ratio and undergo β⁻ decay (ΔZ = +1, ΔN = −1); proton-rich nuclei below the belt undergo β⁺ decay or electron capture (ΔZ = −1, ΔN = +1). Uranium-235 fission fragments inherit a high N/Z ratio (~1.5) far above the stable medium-Z belt (~1.25), so they are neutron-rich and undergo chains of β⁻ decays.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: States stable nuclei follow N = Z up to Z ≈ 20 and bend upward toward N > Z (reaching N/Z ≈ 1.5 near Z = 82).
L1b: States strong nuclear force is short-range (attractive up to ~3 fm, strongly repulsive below ~0.5 fm) acting only on nearest neighbours.
L2a: Explains that electrostatic repulsion between protons is long-range (acts across the whole nucleus) and grows rapidly with Z, requiring a higher N/Z ratio of extra neutrons to bind the nucleus.
L2b: Identifies α emission for heavy nuclei (Z > 82; ΔZ = −2, ΔN = −2) and β⁺ / electron capture below the belt (ΔZ = −1, ΔN = +1).
L3a: Identifies β⁻ emission (explicitly with minus sign!) above the belt (ΔZ = +1, ΔN = −1) converting a neutron to a proton.
L3b: Explains uranium fission fragments lie above the stability belt because they are neutron-rich / have a high N/Z ratio (reject bare 'too many neutrons'), causing successive β⁻ decays.

parts.prompt: Explain the shape of the nuclear stability belt from Z = 0 to Z = 82 in terms of the ranges of the strong nuclear and electrostatic forces, identify how unstable nuclei in each region decay toward stability, and explain why uranium-235 fission fragments are intense β⁻ emitters.
parts.expectedAnswer: above proton number twenty, long-range electrostatic repulsion between all protons grows faster than short-range strong nuclear attraction requiring a higher N/Z ratio. Up to Z ≈ 20, stable nuclei lie along N = Z because each nucleon interacts attractively via the short-range strong nuclear force (attractive up to ~3 fm, strongly repulsive below ~0.5 fm). Above proton number twenty, long-range electrostatic repulsion between all protons grows faster than short-range strong nuclear attraction requiring a higher N/Z ratio, so the stability belt curves upward toward N/Z ≈ 1.5 at Z = 82. Very heavy nuclei (Z > 82) emit α particles (ΔZ = −2, ΔN = −2); neutron-rich nuclei above the belt have a high N/Z ratio and undergo β⁻ decay (ΔZ = +1, ΔN = −1); proton-rich nuclei below the belt undergo β⁺ decay or electron capture (ΔZ = −1, ΔN = +1). Uranium-235 fission fragments inherit a high N/Z ratio (~1.5) far above the stable medium-Z belt (~1.25), so they are neutron-rich and undergo chains of β⁻ decays.
workingSteps: L1: N = Z up to Z ≈ 20, then curves upward to N > Z; state strong nuclear force range (attractive ≤ 3 fm, repulsive < 0.5 fm).
L2: Long-range electrostatic repulsion across all protons vs short-range nearest-neighbour strong attraction explains rising N/Z.
L3: Identify α (Z > 82), β⁻ (above belt, high N/Z), β⁺/EC (below belt), and fission fragments having high N/Z → β⁻.

items.stem: The figure compares a high-energy electron diffraction intensity profile against a Rutherford alpha-particle closest-approach schematic.
items.workedSolution: high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound. In Rutherford closest approach, equating alpha kinetic energy to Coulomb potential energy Eₖ = Q₁Q₂/(4πε₀r_min) yields only an energy-dependent upper bound / overestimate of nuclear radius, because it ignores nuclear recoil and finite alpha size and fails if the alpha gets close enough to interact via the strong nuclear force. By contrast, high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound. Accelerated so λ ~ 10⁻¹⁵ m (comparable to nuclear diameter), electrons produce an intensity-angle curve with a central maximum, a distinctly non-zero first minimum at sin θ ≈ 0.61λ/R, and a smaller secondary peak. Plotting R against A^(1/3) gives R = R₀ A^(1/3); substituting into ρ = Au / [(4/3)πR³] cancels A to yield constant nuclear density ρ = 3u / (4πR₀³) independent of nucleon number.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: Explains Rutherford closest approach converts alpha KE to electrostatic PE (Eₖ = Q₁Q₂ / 4πε₀r_min) giving only an upper bound / overestimate of R.
L1b: States limitations of alpha method: depends on alpha energy, neglects nuclear recoil/finite alpha size, and alpha hadrons experience the strong nuclear force if too close.
L2a: Explains high-energy electrons (λ ~ 10⁻¹⁵ m, comparable to nuclear size) are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force with negligible nuclear recoil.
L2b: Describes electron diffraction graph accurately: intense central maximum, non-zero first minimum at θ_min, and smaller secondary maximum.
L3a: States first minimum satisfies sin θ ≈ 0.61 λ / R, enabling direct measurement of nuclear radius R across isotopes to establish R = R₀ A^(1/3).
L3b: Derives constant nuclear density ρ = Au / [(4/3)πR₀³A] = 3u / (4πR₀³), showing A cancels so nuclear density is constant and independent of mass number.

parts.prompt: Compare how Rutherford alpha closest approach and high-energy electron diffraction determine nuclear radius, explain why electron diffraction is more accurate, describe the features of the diffraction graph, and explain how R = R₀ A^(1/3) proves nuclear density is constant.
parts.expectedAnswer: high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound. In Rutherford closest approach, equating alpha kinetic energy to Coulomb potential energy Eₖ = Q₁Q₂/(4πε₀r_min) yields only an energy-dependent upper bound / overestimate of nuclear radius, because it ignores nuclear recoil and finite alpha size and fails if the alpha gets close enough to interact via the strong nuclear force. By contrast, high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound. Accelerated so λ ~ 10⁻¹⁵ m (comparable to nuclear diameter), electrons produce an intensity-angle curve with a central maximum, a distinctly non-zero first minimum at sin θ ≈ 0.61λ/R, and a smaller secondary peak. Plotting R against A^(1/3) gives R = R₀ A^(1/3); substituting into ρ = Au / [(4/3)πR³] cancels A to yield constant nuclear density ρ = 3u / (4πR₀³) independent of nucleon number.
workingSteps: L1: Alpha closest approach (Eₖ → Q₁Q₂/4πε₀r_min) gives only an upper bound (energy-dependent, recoil, strong force).
L2: High-energy electrons (λ ~ 10⁻¹⁵ m) are leptons (no strong force), giving central max + non-zero first minimum + secondary peak.
L3: sin θ ≈ 0.61λ/R → R = R₀ A^(1/3) → constant nuclear density ρ = 3u/(4πR₀³) independent of A.

items.stem: In 1887, Albert Michelson and Edward Morley attempted to detect Earth's motion through the hypothetical luminiferous ether using an optical interferometer floated on liquid mercury.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 synthesis: splitting coherent light along perpendicular arms and rotating ninety degrees produced a null fringe shift disproving the ether and confirming invariant light speed; covers optical layout, ether-wind transit asymmetry, $90°$ rotation expectation (~0.4 fringe), null observation, and Einstein's invariant-$c$ postulate.

Explains recombined beams interfere in the telescope to produce an observable fringe pattern.
Explains ether-wind hypothesis predicted different round-trip transit times along parallel and perpendicular arms.
Explains rotating the apparatus by $90°$ swaps the arm roles and was expected to shift fringes by a detectable fraction (~0.4 fringe).
States clearly that zero fringe shift (a null result) was observed at all times of day and year.
Links the null result to the non-existence of absolute motion through an ether and Einstein's postulate of invariant light speed $c$.

parts.prompt: Describe the design and operation of the Michelson–Morley interferometer, explain why a fringe shift was expected upon rotating the apparatus by $90°$, and discuss the significance of their null result for Einstein's theory of special relativity.
parts.expectedAnswer: In this landmark experiment, splitting coherent light along perpendicular arms and rotating ninety degrees produced a null fringe shift disproving the ether and confirming invariant light speed. Monochromatic coherent light from a single source strikes a $45°$ semi-silvered beam splitter, dividing into two coherent beams that travel along perpendicular arms of equal length $L$ to mirrors $M_1$ and $M_2$ (a glass compensator plate equalises optical glass path length in both arms). The beams reflect back, recombine at the beam splitter, and enter an observing telescope where they superpose to form bright and dark interference fringes. Assuming Earth moved at orbital speed $v$ through a stationary ether, classical velocity addition predicted unequal round-trip travel times parallel ($\frac{2L/c}{1 - v^2/c^2}$) and perpendicular ($\frac{2L/c}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}$) to the ether wind. Smoothly rotating the granite table by $90°$ on mercury swapped the parallel and perpendicular arms, which was predicted to shift the interference pattern by roughly $0.4$ of a fringe spacing—easily detectable by the apparatus. Despite repeating the measurement at different orientations and seasons, zero fringe shift was ever observed. This null result proved that absolute motion through an ether cannot be detected and led directly to Einstein's postulate that the speed of light in free space is invariant for all inertial observers regardless of source or observer velocity.
workingSteps: Describe interferometer layout: monochromatic source, $45°$ semi-silvered splitter, compensator plate, perpendicular mirrors $M_1, M_2$, telescope.
Explain interference fringes formed by superposition of the two recombined coherent beams.
Explain ether prediction: different round-trip speeds parallel vs perpendicular to Earth's motion through ether.
Explain $90°$ rotation on liquid mercury swapping the two arms and predicting a measurable (~0.4) fringe shift.
State the experimental observation: consistently zero (null) fringe shift across orientations and seasons.
Explain significance: no detectable ether / absolute rest frame and speed of light $c$ is invariant in all inertial frames.

items.stem: During a lanthanide weak-decay spectrometer study, weak quark-flavour transitions (one alpha emission and weak beta-minus transitions (d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ)) convert a parent cerium nucleus with A = 146, Z = 58 into a product nucleus with A = 142, Z = 59.
items.workedSolution: (a) ΔZ = 59 − 58 = 1. Final answer: 1. (b) N₀ = 146 − 58 = 88; N_f = 142 − 59 = 83. ΔN = N_f − N₀ = −5. Final answer: −5. (c) Accounting for ΔA = -4, charge conservation gives 3 weak beta transitions. Final answer: 3.

Computes N = A − Z for parent and daughter and takes N_final − N_parent.
Evaluates correctly to −5.
Links single-quark flavour conversion to ΔZ = ±1 per weak beta step.
Evaluates correctly to 3.

items.stem: Elastic 180° backscattering in a Rutherford backscattering spectrometry (RBS) beamline sends a 4.5 MeV alpha particle (charge +2e) directly toward an immobile platinum target nucleus (Z = 78, A = 195), taking k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Eₖ = 4.5 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 7.20 × 10⁻¹³ J. d = k(2e)(78e) / Eₖ = 4.99 × 10⁻¹⁴ m = 49.9 fm. Final answer: 49.9 fm. (b) R = 1.20 × (195)^(1/3) = 6.96 fm (< d, confirming pure electrostatic scattering). Final answer: 6.96 fm. (c) ρ = (195 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷) / ((4/3)π(6.96 × 10⁻¹⁵)³) = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. Final answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

items.workedSolution: (a) $E_{\text{k(max)}} = 1.94 × 10⁻¹⁹ J$, $V_{\text{s}} = 1.21 V$. (b) Discrete photons interact one to one with surface electrons overcoming the work function; gradient $= h$, intercepts $= f_0$ and $-\phi$, deeper electrons lose extra energy, and doubling intensity doubles photocurrent with unchanged $V_{\text{s}}$.

Obtain $E_{\text{k(max)}} = 1.94 × 10⁻¹⁹ J$.
Obtain $V_{\text{s}} = 1.21 V$.
L1 (Area 1): Identifies gradient of both parallel lines as Planck constant h.
L1 (Area 1): Identifies x-intercept as threshold frequency f₀ and vertical intercept magnitude as work function φ.
L2 (Area 2): States one-to-one photon-electron interaction (E = hf) overcoming minimum surface energy φ.
L2 (Area 2): Explains surface electrons escape with Ek(max) while deeper electrons lose extra energy overcoming internal bonds/collisions.
L3 (Area 3): Links stopping potential strictly to maximum kinetic energy (eVs = Ek(max)), unchanged at fixed frequency.
L3 (Area 3): Explains doubling intensity doubles photons per second -> doubles rate of photoelectron emission / photocurrent while Vs stays unchanged.
