options.label: D
options.text: Because alpha particles are massless leptons whose closest approach underestimates the true nuclear radius.
options.distractorRationale: Alpha particles are composite hadrons (helium-4 nuclei) and r_min overestimates (upper bound) the nuclear radius.

Concludes speed approaches $c$ asymptotically and no finite energy reaches $c$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the Lorentz factor $\gamma$ of the electrons.
Calculate the relativistic kinetic energy of one electron in joules.
Explain why no finite accelerating potential difference can ever accelerate an electron to $v = c$.
parts.expectedAnswer: Because $\gamma \to \infty$ as $v \to c$, infinite energy would be required; consequently, electron speed approaches the speed of light asymptotically as kinetic energy increases rather than following the classical straight line.
workingSteps: As $v \to c$, $\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} \to 0$ so $E_k = (\gamma - 1) m_0 c^2 \to \infty$.
Hence $c$ is an unattainable upper speed limit for any particle with non-zero rest mass.

items.stem: Within a cyclotron-produced PET calibration parent chain, a germanium isotope of nucleon number 68 and proton number 32 decays by purely weak beta-plus transitions (u → d + e⁺ + νₑ) to a nuclide with A = 68 and Z = 30.
items.workedSolution: (a) ΔZ = 30 − 32 = −2. Final answer: −2. (b) N₀ = 68 − 32 = 36; N_f = 68 − 30 = 38. ΔN = N_f − N₀ = 2. Final answer: 2. (c) Accounting for ΔA = 0, charge conservation gives 2 weak beta transitions. Final answer: 2.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Z_final − Z_parent with sign to obtain −2.
Computes N = A − Z for parent and daughter and takes N_final − N_parent.
Evaluates correctly to 2.
Links single-quark flavour conversion to ΔZ = ±1 per weak beta step.
Evaluates correctly to 2.

items.stem: In a heavy-element Coulomb-barrier scattering rig, an energetic proton (charge +1e) with initial kinetic energy 5.1 MeV approaches a stationary lead nucleus (Z = 82, A = 208) directly head-on and recoils elastically. Neglect target recoil and take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Eₖ = 5.1 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 8.16 × 10⁻¹³ J. d = k(1e)(82e) / Eₖ = 2.31 × 10⁻¹⁴ m = 23.1 fm. Final answer: 23.1 fm. (b) R = 1.20 × (208)^(1/3) = 7.11 fm (< d, confirming pure electrostatic scattering). Final answer: 7.11 fm. (c) ρ = (208 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷) / ((4/3)π(7.11 × 10⁻¹⁵)³) = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. Final answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

items.stem: A negatively charged clean zinc plate on a gold-leaf electroscope discharges instantly under dim ultraviolet light, yet remains charged indefinitely under intense visible light.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 (5–6 marks): Explains why wave theory fails (predicts emission at any frequency with delay and intensity-dependent KE); states that discrete photons interact one to one with surface electrons overcoming the work function ($E = hf \ge \phi$); links $E_{\text{k(max)}} = hf - \phi = eV_{\text{s}}$ and intensity = photon arrival rate (electrons emitted from zinc plate, never gold leaf).

markScheme.criterion: L1 (Area 1): Wave theory predicts emission at any frequency once electrons gradually accumulate enough energy, contradicting the existence of threshold frequency f₀ and instantaneous emission.
L1 (Area 1): Wave theory predicts photoelectron kinetic energy should increase with intensity, contradicting observation that Ek(max) depends on frequency.
L2 (Area 2): Photon model states EM radiation consists of discrete packets (photons) of energy E = hf.
L2 (Area 2): One-to-one interaction: a single surface electron absorbs all the energy of one single photon and escapes only if hf >= φ (work function).
L3 (Area 3): Applies Ek(max) = hf − φ = eVs, explicitly stating maximum kinetic energy depends only on frequency and work function.

L3 (Area 3): Explains that increasing intensity (for f >= f₀) increases number of photons arriving per second, emitting more photoelectrons per second from the zinc plate (reject 'from gold leaf') so photocurrent / rate of leaf fall increases.

parts.prompt: Explain why the classical wave theory of light fails to account for these photoelectric observations, and explain how Einstein's photon model accounts for threshold frequency, maximum photoelectron kinetic energy, and the effect of increasing intensity above threshold.
parts.expectedAnswer: Wave theory predicts continuous energy delivery spread across the wavefront so electrons should accumulate energy and escape at any frequency after a time delay, and maximum kinetic energy should rise with intensity—both contradicted by experiment. In the photon model, discrete photons interact one to one with surface electrons overcoming the work function: each photon carries $E = hf$, and a single electron absorbs all of one photon's energy instantly, escaping only if $hf \ge \phi$ (defining threshold frequency $f_0 = \phi/h$). Excess energy gives $E_{\text{k(max)}} = hf - \phi = eV_{\text{s}}$, depending solely on $f$ and $\phi$, while higher intensity at $f \ge f_0$ delivers more photons per second so more photoelectrons are emitted from the zinc plate per second and the leaf falls faster.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): Contrast wave prediction (emission at any f after delay; Ek increases with intensity) with observed threshold f₀ and instant emission.
Area 2 (L2): State photon packets E = hf, one-to-one interaction, and surface work function threshold hf >= φ.
Area 3 (L3): Link Ek(max) = hf − φ = eVs (must state 'maximum' KE) and explain higher intensity = more photons/s -> greater current / faster discharge from zinc plate.

items.stem: To verify wave-particle duality, a 2250 V electron beam is directed perpendicularly onto ultrathin polycrystalline platinum foil (d = 2.27 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) at distance L = 0.19 m from a detector screen. Take first-order ring geometry sin θ = λ / d and r = L tan θ, with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) p = √(2mₑeV) = 2.56 × 10⁻²³ N s. λ = h / p = 2.59 × 10⁻¹¹ m = 25.9 pm. Final answer: 25.9 pm. (b) sin θ = λ / d = 2.59 × 10⁻¹¹ / (2.27 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) = 0.114. θ = 6.55 °. Final answer: 6.55 °. (c) r = L tan θ = 0.19 × tan(6.55°) = 0.0218 m. Final answer: 0.0218 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ = h / √(2mₑeV) with SI values and converts to picometres.
Evaluates correctly to 25.9 pm.
Applies sin θ = λ / d and converts to degrees.
Evaluates correctly to 6.55 °.
Evaluates r = L tan θ using the screen distance L.
Evaluates correctly to 0.0218 m.

items.workedSolution: (a) R = 1.20 × (184)^(1/3) = 6.83 fm. Final answer: 6.83 fm. (b) R = 6.83 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Final answer: 6.83 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. (c) m = 184 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; V = (4/3)π(6.83 × 10⁻¹⁵)³. ρ = m / V = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. Final answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

Evaluates correctly to 6.83 fm.

Evaluates correctly to 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

items.stem: Spectroscopic analysis of argon gas in an inductively coupled argon plasma spectrometer places the ground level at −15.7 eV and a neighbouring bound state at −4.18 eV, taking free electrons at rest to have zero energy. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the longest wavelength of electromagnetic radiation capable of ionizing an atom directly from the ground level?
items.workedSolution: Ionization from the ground level requires ΔE = 0 − (−15.7) = 15.7 eV = 2.51 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. Maximum wavelength λ = hc / ΔE = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸) / (2.51 × 10⁻¹⁸) = 79.2 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Converts ΔE = 15.7 eV to joules and applies λ = hc / ΔE to obtain 79.2 nm (C).

items.stem: A TEM operator increases the accelerating anode potential difference from 25.0 kV to 100 kV. Ignoring relativistic effects, what is the ratio $\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}$ of the new electron de Broglie wavelength to the original wavelength?
items.workedSolution: Since $\lambda \propto V^{-1/2}$, increasing $V$ by a factor of 4 multiplies $\lambda$ by $\sqrt{\frac{25.0}{100}} = 0.500$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 0.500.

items.stem: Before testing a fluorine-18 sample (half-life 110 min) in a PET radiopharmacy quality-control well counter, ambient background radiation registers 38 counts min⁻¹. Introducing the source raises the total detector reading to 230 counts min⁻¹ initially, and monitoring continues for an elapsed interval of 220 min. What total count rate (including background) does the detector record at t = 220 min?
items.workedSolution: Initial net count rate C₀ = 230 − 38 = 192 counts min⁻¹. Number of half-lives n = 220 / 110 = 2. Remaining net count rate C = 192 / 2^2 = 48 counts min⁻¹. Total recorded count rate = 48 + 38 = 86.0 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background (192), divides by 2^2 (48), and adds 38 back to obtain 86.0 counts min⁻¹ (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides the initial total count rate directly by 2ⁿ without subtracting the background count rate first.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Correctly halves the background-subtracted net count rate but forgets to add the background count rate back to obtain the total detector reading.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Halves the uncorrected count rate first and subtracts the background count rate at the end.

items.stem: In a leukocyte-labelling nuclear medicine lab, a radiochemist prepares 2.4 × 10¹³ radioactive nuclei of indium-111 (half-life T₁/₂ = 2.8 d) and measures the sample again after an elapsed time of 6.1 d. What is the initial activity A₀ of the sample, in Bq, at t = 0?
items.workedSolution: Converting half-life to SI seconds: T₁/₂ = 2.8 × 86400 = 2.42 × 10⁵ s. Decay constant λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂ = 2.87 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹. Initial activity A₀ = λN₀ = 6.88 × 10⁷ Bq.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates λ = ln 2 / (2.8 × 86400) and A₀ = λN₀ = 6.88 × 10⁷ Bq (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Leaves T₁/₂ in d instead of converting to seconds when evaluating A₀ = (ln 2 / T₁/₂) N₀ in Bq.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor ln 2 ≈ 0.693 in λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the decayed activity at elapsed time t instead of A₀ at t = 0.

items.stem: A negative kaon ($S = -1$) decays into two pions ($S = 0$): $K^- \to \pi^- + \pi^0$. Which interaction must be responsible for this decay?
items.workedSolution: Because strangeness changes ($\Delta S = +1$) while $Q$ and $B$ are conserved, this must be a weak interaction because strangeness changes (AQA requires stating explicitly that strangeness changes here). Therefore option C is correct: weak interaction because strangeness changes.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: weak interaction because strangeness changes.

items.stem: Which physical process allows a PET ring scanner to determine the line of response passing through a tumour?
items.workedSolution: Conservation of momentum and energy means an emitted positron annihilates with an electron producing two opposite 511 keV gamma photons detected in coincidence, defining a straight line of response across the ring.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that emitted positron annihilates with an electron producing two opposite 511 keV gamma photons detected in coincidence.

items.stem: A classroom ceiling light uses a low-pressure mercury fluorescent tube whose glass wall is lined on the inside with a phosphor coating.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 (5–6 marks): Colliding free electrons excite mercury orbital electrons emitting ultraviolet photons absorbed by phosphor coating; links acceleration -> collisional excitation of orbital electrons -> discrete UV de-excitation ($hf = E_1 - E_2$) -> phosphor absorption -> multi-step cascade emitting visible wavelengths.

markScheme.criterion: L1 (Area 1): High potential difference accelerates free electrons through the low-pressure mercury vapour.
L1 (Area 1): Free electrons collide inelastically with atomic orbital electrons in mercury atoms, exciting them to higher discrete energy levels (or ionising to supply more free electrons).
L2 (Area 2): Excited mercury electrons rapidly de-excite / fall back to lower discrete energy levels.
L2 (Area 2): Each downward transition emits a discrete photon of energy hf = E₁ − E₂ predominantly in the ultraviolet (UV) region.
L3 (Area 3): Inner phosphor coating absorbs the UV photons, exciting orbital electrons in the coating atoms.
L3 (Area 3): Coating electrons de-excite in multiple smaller steps (cascades) through intermediate levels, emitting lower-energy / longer-wavelength visible photons.

parts.prompt: Explain in detail how a fluorescent tube emits visible light when a high potential difference is applied across its ends. In your answer, explain the processes of excitation/ionisation in mercury vapour, ultraviolet photon emission, and the role of the phosphor coating.
parts.expectedAnswer: A high potential difference accelerates free electrons along the tube; colliding free electrons excite mercury orbital electrons emitting ultraviolet photons absorbed by phosphor coating. Specifically, inelastic collisions transfer kinetic energy to atomic orbital electrons in mercury atoms, exciting them to higher discrete energy levels (or ionising mercury atoms to maintain the flow of free electrons). Excited mercury electrons quickly de-excite to lower discrete energy levels, emitting photons of energy $hf = E_1 - E_2$ predominantly in the ultraviolet region. The inner phosphor coating absorbs these UV photons, exciting phosphor atoms, whose electrons then de-excite via multiple smaller downward transitions (cascades) through intermediate levels, emitting lower-energy, longer-wavelength visible photons across many colours.
workingSteps: Area 1 (L1): High p.d. accelerates free electrons; collisions with atomic orbital electrons excite/ionise mercury atoms.
Area 2 (L2): Excited mercury electrons de-excite to lower discrete levels, emitting discrete UV photons with hf = E₁ − E₂.
Area 3 (L3): Phosphor absorbs UV photons and de-excites via multiple smaller step cascades, emitting lower-energy/longer-wavelength visible photons.

items.stem: Spectra recorded from an X-ray binary accretion-disc corona show five-times ionized carbon C⁵⁺ (Z = 6) whose bound levels follow Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV relative to the ionization continuum. Consider ions prepared in excited shell n = 3 (with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).
items.workedSolution: (a) Eₙ = −13.6 × (6)² / (3)² = −54.4 eV. Ionization energy ΔE = 0 − Eₙ = 54.4 eV. Final answer: 54.4 eV. (b) ΔE = 54.4 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 8.70 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. f = ΔE / h = 8.70 × 10⁻¹⁸ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 1.31 × 10¹⁶ Hz. Final answer: 1.31 × 10¹⁶ Hz. (c) λ = (3.00 × 10⁸) / (1.31 × 10¹⁶) = 22.9 nm. Final answer: 22.9 nm.

Evaluates correctly to 54.4 eV.
Converts ionization energy from eV to J and divides by Planck's constant h.
Evaluates correctly to 1.31 × 10¹⁶ Hz.
Uses λ = c / f and expresses the wavelength in nm to obtain 22.9 nm.

items.stem: Energy-balance modelling of a magnetic-confinement tokamak D–T plasma burn considers deuterium–tritium fusion: deuteron (A = 2, Z = 1, mass 2.013553 u) + triton (A = 3, Z = 1, mass 3.015501 u) → helium nucleus (A = 4, Z = 2, mass 4.001506 u) + neutron (mass 1.008665 u). items.workedSolution: Mass decrease Δm = Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 0.0189 u. Energy released Q = Δm × 931.5 = 17.6 MeV.

markScheme.criterion: Computes Δm = 0.0189 u and Q = Δm × 931.5 = 17.6 MeV (A).

items.stem: When a slow-moving electron and positron meet and annihilate, why are two gamma photons produced rather than a single gamma photon?
items.workedSolution: Initial net momentum is nearly zero, so two gamma photons travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum (reject 'elimination'; always say annihilation and positron). Therefore option C is correct: two gamma photons travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: two gamma photons travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum.

options.label: A
options.text: To conserve linear momentum, a single photon splits into an electron and positron along the same line
options.distractorRationale: Describes pair production rather than annihilation, and still does not balance zero initial momentum.

options.label: B
options.text: To conserve linear momentum, two gamma photons travel in the same direction at half the speed of light
options.distractorRationale: Photons always travel at c in vacuum and parallel photons would carry non-zero net momentum.

options.label: C
options.text: To conserve linear momentum, two gamma photons travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum

options.label: D
options.text: To conserve linear momentum, one photon carries positive charge and the other carries negative charge
options.distractorRationale: Gamma photons are electrically neutral.

options.label: A
options.text: Because alpha particles travel faster than light and bypass the GM tube dead time.
options.distractorRationale: Alpha particles are massive, slow, strongly ionising, and stopped by ~5 cm of air.

options.label: B
options.text: Because gamma rays are deflected magnetically into a parallel non-diverging beam.
options.distractorRationale: Gamma rays are uncharged EM photons radiating isotropically (1/r² geometric spreading).

options.label: C
options.text: Gamma rays are negligibly absorbed in air over 0.1–0.6 m whereas alpha range is only a few cm; always handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset.

options.label: D
options.text: Because sealed gamma sources are harmless outside lead storage boxes.
options.distractorRationale: Gamma radiation is highly penetrating and requires strict ALARA controls (time, distance, shielding, tongs).

items.stem: A bare lithium-7 nucleus ($^{7}_{3}\mathrm{Li}$) is studied in a particle accelerator. Take $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, $m_{\text{p}} = 1.673 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, and $m_{\text{n}} = 1.675 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $N = 7 - 3 = 4$. (b) $m = 1.172 × 10⁻²⁶ kg$, $Q = 4.80 × 10⁻¹⁹ C$, so $Q/m = 4.10 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹$. (c) neutrons contribute mass without adding electric charge.

markScheme.criterion: Correct neutron number $N = 4$.
Calculate total mass $m = 1.17 × 10⁻²⁶ kg$ including both protons and neutrons.
Substitute net charge $Q = 4.80 × 10⁻¹⁹ C$ into $Q/m$.
Obtain specific charge $= 4.10 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹$.
State that neutrons contribute mass without adding electric charge.

parts.prompt: State the number of neutrons in the Li nucleus.
Calculate the total mass of the species in kilograms and hence determine the magnitude of its specific charge.
Explain why neutral neutrons affect the specific charge of a nucleus or ion.
parts.expectedAnswer: Although neutrons carry zero charge, neutrons contribute mass without adding electric charge, increasing the mass denominator and lowering $Q/m$.
workingSteps: Link unchanged charge and larger denominator mass to smaller specific charge.

items.stem: When plotting scattered electron intensity against scattering angle θ from a thin carbon target, why does the curve dip to a non-zero first minimum rather than touching zero, and why are electrons chosen over alpha particles?
items.workedSolution: High-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound. Therefore the correct statement is: Scattering overlays diffraction so the dip stays above zero, and high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound.

options.text: The intensity touches zero strictly at θ = 90° because electrons undergo strong-force capture inside the nucleus.
options.distractorRationale: Electrons do not interact via the strong force and the first minimum is non-zero at sin θ ≈ 0.61λ/R.

options.label: B
options.text: Electrons are chosen solely because they carry positive charge and match the alpha particle's mass.
options.distractorRationale: Electrons are negatively charged leptons ~7300 times lighter than alpha particles.

options.label: C
options.text: Alpha particles give exact nuclear radii while electrons only provide rough upper bounds.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the relative accuracy of the two methods.

options.label: D
options.text: Scattering overlays diffraction so the dip stays above zero, and high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound

items.stem: If power sensors detect that the average number of neutrons per fission causing another fission has drifted above one, how does the emergency shutdown system halt the chain reaction?
items.workedSolution: Fully inserting boron or cadmium control rods absorb neutrons to maintain a steady critical chain reaction (and drop k below 1 for shutdown). Therefore the correct statement is: Fully inserting boron or cadmium control rods absorb neutrons to maintain a steady critical chain reaction

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: boron or cadmium control rods absorb neutrons to maintain a steady critical chain reaction.

options.distractorRationale: Graphite moderates (slows) neutrons to promote fission rather than absorbing them.

items.stem: In Bertozzi's experiment measuring electron time-of-flight speed against accelerating kinetic energy up to several MeV, how did the experimental data refute classical mechanics?
items.workedSolution: Direct speed and calorimeter measurements confirmed $E_k = (\gamma - 1) m_0 c^2$ as electron speed approaches the speed of light asymptotically as kinetic energy increases rather than following the classical straight line.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that electron speed approaches the speed of light asymptotically as kinetic energy increases rather than following the classical straight line.

options.label: A
options.text: Electron speed increased linearly with kinetic energy far beyond the speed of light.
options.distractorRationale: Linear v^2 vs E_k surpassing c^2 was the failed classical prediction, not Bertozzi's result.

options.label: B
options.text: Electron kinetic energy dropped to zero once electrons exceeded half the speed of light.
options.distractorRationale: Calorimetry at the aluminium target verified that electrons carried the full relativistic kinetic energy.

options.label: C
options.text: Electron speed peaked at half the speed of light and then decreased at higher accelerating voltages.
options.distractorRationale: Speed increases monotonically, approaching c asymptotically.

options.label: D
options.text: Bertozzi's graph demonstrated that electron speed approaches the speed of light asymptotically as kinetic energy increases rather than following the classical straight line.

items.stem: In a fuel-cladding activation beta-minus sequence, a parent zirconium nucleus (A = 95, Z = 40) transforms via purely weak beta-minus transitions (d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ) into a final nuclide with A = 95 and Z = 42, conserving baryon and lepton numbers at every vertex. What is the signed net change in neutron number ΔN = N_final − N_parent across the sequence?
items.workedSolution: Initial neutron number N₀ = 95 − 40 = 55; final neutron number N_f = 95 − 42 = 53. Thus ΔN = N_f − N₀ = −2.

markScheme.criterion: Uses N = A − Z to obtain ΔN = (95 − 42) − (95 − 40) = −2 (A).

items.stem: Elastic 180° backscattering in a refractory-foil elastic alpha-scattering chamber sends a 4.2 MeV alpha particle (charge +2e) directly toward an immobile tungsten target nucleus (Z = 74, A = 184), taking k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the distance of closest approach d, in femtometres (fm)?
items.workedSolution: Initial kinetic energy Eₖ = 4.2 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.72 × 10⁻¹³ J. At the turning point, Eₖ = k(2e)(74e) / d, so d = (8.99 × 10⁹)(2)(74)(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)² / 6.72 × 10⁻¹³ = 50.7 fm.

markScheme.criterion: Equates Eₖ to k Q₁ Q₂ / d to obtain d = 50.7 fm (B).

items.stem: Within a targeted alpha-immunotherapy generator column, heavy actinium nuclei of mass number 227 and atomic number 89 undergo alpha and beta-minus steps to reach A = 211, Z = 83. What is the net change in neutron number ΔN = N_final − N_parent across the entire chain?
items.workedSolution: Parent neutron number N₀ = 227 − 89 = 138. Final neutron number N_f = 211 − 83 = 128. Therefore ΔN = N_f − N₀ = −10.

items.stem: The graph shows maximum photoelectron kinetic energy $E_{\text{k(max)}}$ plotted against incident frequency $f$ for two different clean metals A and B. Why are the two straight lines parallel?
items.workedSolution: Rearranging $E_{\text{k(max)}} = hf - \phi$ shows the gradient equals the Planck constant $h$ for every metal surface. Therefore option B is correct: gradient equals the Planck constant for every metal surface.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: gradient equals the Planck constant for every metal surface.

options.text: The lines have identical slope because the gradient equals the elementary charge divided by Planck constant
options.distractorRationale: Inverts h/e; on an Ek(max)–f graph the gradient is h (and on a Vs–f graph it is h/e).

options.text: The lines have identical slope because both metals share the same threshold frequency
options.distractorRationale: The horizontal intercepts f₀A and f₀B are distinct because the metals have different work functions.

items.stem: Within a Thomson-type diffraction bulb, 320 V electrons traverse thin polycrystalline nickel foil whose crystal planes are separated by d = 2.03 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, illuminating a ring on a screen L = 0.18 m away (sin θ = λ / d, r = L tan θ, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). What is the first-order diffraction angle θ, in degrees?
items.workedSolution: Electron wavelength λ = h / √(2mₑeV) = 6.86 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Using sin θ = λ / d = 0.338 yields θ = arcsin(0.338) = 19.8 °.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates λ = h / √(2mₑeV) and θ = arcsin(λ / d) = 19.8 ° (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Leaves arcsin(λ / d) in radians while labelling the answer in degrees.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Inserts an extra factor of 2 in the denominator despite sin θ = λ / d being specified.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 in p = √(2mₑeV) when computing the electron de Broglie wavelength.

items.stem: During a charge-distribution scattering experiment, a 5.2 MeV alpha beam (charge +2e) probes calcium-40 nuclei (Z = 20, A = 40). Assume a uniform spherical nucleus obeying R = R₀ A^(1/3), where R₀ = 1.20 fm = 1.20 × 10⁻¹⁵ m and u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Assuming nuclear mass m ≈ A u, what is the nuclear matter density ρ of this calcium-40 nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Since R = R₀ A^(1/3), V = (4/3)πR³ = (4/3)π R₀³ A. Thus ρ = (A u) / ((4/3)π R₀³ A) = 3u / (4π R₀³) = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Computes ρ = A u / ((4/3)πR³) = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³ (C).

items.stem: The energy-level diagram illustrates radiative transitions in helium gas within a stellar chromosphere helium absorption cell. An atom initially occupies the second excited state at energy −3.39 eV (with a nearby level at −4.8 eV and ionization at zero eV). Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) ΔE = 0 − (−3.39) = 3.39 eV. Final answer: 3.39 eV. (b) ΔE = 3.39 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 5.42 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. f = ΔE / h = 5.42 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 8.18 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Final answer: 8.18 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (c) λ = c / f = (3.00 × 10⁸) / (8.18 × 10¹⁴) = 3.67 × 10⁻⁷ m. Converting to nanometres gives λ = 367 nm. Final answer: 367 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds ΔE = 0 − E_initial in eV to obtain 3.39 eV.
Converts ΔE to joules (× 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) and applies f = ΔE / h.
Evaluates correctly to 8.18 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
Uses λ = c / f (or hc / ΔE) and converts metres to nanometres.
Evaluates correctly to 367 nm.

parts.prompt: Compare the wave-particle operating principles, image-formation methods, and practical limitations of a TEM and an STM.
parts.expectedAnswer: Both microscopes harness electron wave behaviour in distinct ways: TEM uses high accelerating potential to shorten electron de Broglie wavelength while STM uses exponential quantum tunnelling sensitivity across a nanometre gap. In a TEM, an electron gun accelerates electrons through tens to hundreds of kilovolts so $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2m_e e V}$ becomes picometres—far shorter than visible light—reducing diffraction limits. Magnetic condenser, objective, and projector lenses focus the beam through an ultra-thin specimen in vacuum onto a fluorescent screen or sensor, where denser regions scatter more electrons and appear darker. However, TEM resolution is practically limited because specimens must be extremely thin (thicker samples slow electrons, increasing $\lambda$ and blurring focus), electrons leave the filament with a spread of speeds, and magnetic lenses exhibit spherical/chromatic-like aberrations. In an STM, a needle-fine conducting tip hovers roughly $1\text{ nm}$ above a conducting sample with a small bias voltage. Electrons cross the forbidden vacuum gap via quantum tunnelling because their wavefunctions penetrate the barrier, with tunnelling current decaying exponentially with gap width $d$. Scanning in constant-current mode (using piezoelectric feedback to track surface relief) or constant-height mode maps individual surface atoms directly, though the STM is restricted to conducting or semiconducting surfaces, requires extreme vibration isolation, and maps surface electron clouds rather than internal bulk structure.
workingSteps: Explain TEM wave principle: high anode pd gives picometre de Broglie wavelength $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2m_e eV}$, minimising diffraction.
Describe TEM image formation: magnetic condenser/objective/projector lenses transmitting electrons through ultra-thin sample in vacuum.
State TEM limitations: ultra-thin specimens needed (thickness slows electrons increasing $\lambda$), lens aberrations, and electron speed spread.
Explain STM wave principle: electron wavefunction penetrates narrow vacuum barrier (quantum tunnelling) with exponential gap sensitivity.
Describe STM scanning: piezo-controlled constant-current feedback or constant-height current mapping.
State STM limitations: requires conducting samples, ultra-stable vibration isolation, and probes only the surface layer.

items.stem: A radiation detector in an environmental air-filter beta counter operates in a steady background of 26 counts min⁻¹. A fresh bismuth-214 specimen with half-life 19.9 min gives an initial uncorrected reading of 306 counts min⁻¹. Consider the detector response after 59.7 min.
items.workedSolution: (a) C₀,net = 306 − 26 = 280 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 280 counts min⁻¹. (b) n = 59.7 / 19.9 = 3 half-lives. C_net = 280 / 2^3 = 35.0 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 35.0 counts min⁻¹. (c) C_total = 34.99999999999999 + 26 = 61.0 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 61.0 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background count rate from initial total count rate to obtain 280 counts min⁻¹.
Identifies 3 elapsed half-lives and divides initial net count rate by 2^3.
Evaluates correctly to 35.0 counts min⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Compare CT, MRI, and Ultrasound imaging across physical operating principles, image contrast and resolution, ionising radiation risk, and practical clinical limitations or contraindications.
parts.expectedAnswer: Clinicians select imaging modalities by balancing contrast, safety, and availability: MRI provides non-ionising high soft tissue contrast CT gives detailed X-ray slices with ionising dose and ultrasound is safe portable and real time. CT rotates an X-ray tube and detector ring around the patient to reconstruct crisp 3D cross-sections of dense bone and acute internal bleeding, but delivers a substantial ionising X-ray dose that restricts repeated use and pregnancy scanning. MRI aligns hydrogen protons in a strong superconducting magnetic field, excites them with radiofrequency pulses at the Larmor frequency, and detects relaxation signals to distinguish subtle soft-tissue and brain structures without ionising radiation; however, MRI scanners are costly, slow, noisy, claustrophobic, cannot image dry cortical bone well (few free hydrogen protons), and are strictly contraindicated for patients with ferromagnetic implants or unshielded pacemakers. Diagnostic ultrasound uses high-frequency longitudinal acoustic pulses reflected at impedance boundaries, making it completely non-ionising, inexpensive, portable, and ideal for real-time fetal and cardiac imaging, though it offers lower resolution, cannot penetrate bone or air-filled lungs due to near-total reflection, and requires skilled operator interpretation.
workingSteps: Explain CT: rotating X-ray slices, high bone/trauma resolution, significant ionising dose.
Explain MRI: strong B-field + RF Larmor excitation of hydrogen protons, zero ionising risk, superior soft-tissue/brain contrast.
State MRI limitations: expensive, slow, poor dry-bone signal, hazardous with ferromagnetic implants/pacemakers.
Explain Ultrasound: non-ionising acoustic pulse-echo reflection, portable, low-cost, real-time imaging.
State Ultrasound limitations: blocked by bone and air pockets (impedance mismatch), lower spatial detail.
Synthesise clinical selection (e.g. ultrasound for pregnancy, MRI for brain/ligaments, CT for rapid bone/trauma).

items.stem: An atom has $5$ distinct bound energy levels available during de-excitation from the highest state down to the ground state. Assuming all transitions have different energy gaps, how many distinct spectral emission wavelengths can be produced?
items.workedSolution: The number of downward pairs among $n = 5$ levels is $n(n - 1)/2 = 5 \times 4 / 2 = 10.0$ distinct lines. Option D (10.0) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Distinct emission lines $= 10$ (10.0, option D).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates γ = 1 / √(1 − v²/c²).
Evaluates correctly to 1.57.
Applies tan θ = |v| / c and converts arctan(|v|/c) to degrees.
Evaluates correctly to 37.6 °.
Applies u′ = (u − v) / (1 − uv/c²) preserving algebraic signs.
Evaluates correctly to −0.982.

items.stem: Within a laser-produced ablation plasma plume, one-electron four-times ionized boron B⁴⁺ (Z = 5) ions populate principal shell n = 1 under the Bohr scaling law Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV relative to zero continuum energy (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). What minimum photon frequency is needed to remove the electron completely from principal shell n = 1?
items.workedSolution: Ionization energy from n = 1 is ΔE = 13.6 × 5² / 1² = 340 eV = 5.44 × 10⁻¹⁷ J. Threshold frequency f = ΔE / h = 8.21 × 10¹⁶ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates f = (13.6 Z² / n²)(e / h) = 8.21 × 10¹⁶ Hz (D).

items.stem: Evaluating strong-force binding in a liquid-metal fast-reactor coolant data sheet, a fully stripped sodium-23 nucleus (proton number Z = 11, nucleon number A = 23) has rest mass 22.983733 u. Constants: mₚ = 1.007276 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u, u = 931.5 MeV c⁻². What is the binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, of this sodium-23 nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Neutron count N = 23 − 11 = 12. Mass defect Δm = 11(1.007276) + 12(1.008665) − 22.983733 = 0.200 u. Total binding energy B = Δm × 931.5 = 187 MeV. Binding energy per nucleon B / A = 187 / 23 = 8.11 MeV.

markScheme.criterion: Computes Δm = 0.200 u, B = 187 MeV, and B / A = 8.11 MeV (D).

items.stem: In a low-energy electron diffraction (LEED) gun, a collimated stream of electrons is accelerated from rest by a 4200 V supply. Constants: h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the de Broglie wavelength, in picometres (pm), of the electrons?
items.workedSolution: Kinetic energy Eₖ = qV = 6.72 × 10⁻¹⁶ J. Momentum p = √(2mEₖ) = 3.50 × 10⁻²³ N s. De Broglie wavelength λ = h / p = 18.9 pm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates p and λ = h / p to obtain 18.9 pm (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 inside p = √(2mEₖ), computing λ = h / √(mEₖ).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the elementary charge factor e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C when converting accelerating voltage to joules.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats the massive particle as a massless photon using λ = hc / E instead of λ = h / p.

items.stem: A hospital CT scanner tube accelerates electrons across 110 kV onto a rotating tungsten target embedded in a copper block. Take $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$, $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $E_{\max} = 1.76 × 10⁻¹⁴ J$. (b) $\lambda_{\min} = 11.3 pm$. (c) increasing anode voltage reduces minimum wavelength and raises intensity while characteristic peak wavelengths stay fixed.

markScheme.criterion: Uses $E = eV = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.10 \times 10^5$.
Correct energy 1.76 × 10⁻¹⁴ J.
Evaluates $\lambda_{\min} = hc / E_{\max}$.
Correct wavelength 11.3 pm.
States $\lambda_{\min}$ shifts shorter and continuum intensity increases.
States characteristic K-line wavelengths remain unchanged.

parts.prompt: Calculate the maximum kinetic energy in joules of an electron striking the tungsten anode.
Calculate the corresponding minimum X-ray wavelength in picometres.
State how the X-ray emission spectrum changes if the anode voltage is raised from 110 kV to 130 kV at constant filament current.
parts.expectedAnswer: Raising the potential difference means increasing anode voltage reduces minimum wavelength and raises intensity while characteristic peak wavelengths stay fixed.
workingSteps: Minimum wavelength decreases ($lambda_{\min} \propto 1/V$) and overall intensity rises.
Characteristic tungsten K-line wavelengths remain strictly unchanged.

items.stem: Reaction kinematics in a linear-accelerator proton–lithium target experiment examine proton–lithium-7 Cockcroft–Walton fusion, where bare rest masses satisfy proton (1.007276 u) + lithium-7 nucleus (7.014358 u) → 2 alpha particles (each of mass 4.001506 u). Assume 1 u = 931.5 MeV c⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Δm = Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 0.0186 u. Final answer: 0.0186 u. (b) Q = 0.0186 × 931.5 = 17.3 MeV. Final answer: 17.3 MeV. (c) Total nucleon number A = 8. Final answer: 8.

markScheme.criterion: Sums all reactant and product rest masses including particle multiplicities.
Evaluates correctly to 0.0186 u.
Multiplies Δm in u by 931.5 MeV u⁻¹.
Evaluates correctly to 17.3 MeV.
Sums nucleon numbers across reactants (or products) to obtain 8.

items.stem: Monochromatic electromagnetic radiation of frequency 2.87 × 10¹⁵ Hz strikes an oxygen-free copper accelerator photocathode whose work function is 4.7 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the maximum kinetic energy, in electron-volts (eV), of the emitted photoelectrons?
items.workedSolution: Incident photon energy E = hf / e = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 2.87 × 10¹⁵) / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 11.9 eV. Subtracting Φ = 4.7 eV gives Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 7.19 eV.

markScheme.criterion: Converts hf to eV and subtracts Φ = 4.7 eV to obtain 7.19 eV (A).

items.stem: Monochromatic photons of wavelength 208 nm eject photoelectrons in vacuum from a degassed calcium photoemission electrode (calcium, Φ = 2.87 eV). Assume h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. What is the maximum speed of the emitted photoelectrons?
items.workedSolution: Incident photon energy E = hc / λ = 9.56 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; work function Φ = 2.87 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.59 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Thus Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, giving vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ) = 1.04 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = hc/λ − Φ and vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ) = 1.04 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: In a PET medical scanner, a positron and an electron with combined kinetic energy $0.28\text{ MeV}$ annihilate to produce two gamma photons. Rest energy $= 0.511\text{ MeV}$, $1\text{ MeV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$, $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$.
items.workedSolution: (a) Each photon has $E = 0.651 MeV$, giving $f = 1.57 × 10²⁰ Hz$. (b) two gamma photons travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum.

markScheme.criterion: Each photon energy $= 0.651 MeV$.
Convert photon energy to joules and apply $f = E/h$.
Frequency $= 1.57 × 10²⁰ Hz$.
Momentum must be conserved (initial momentum ~ 0).
Two gamma photons travel in opposite directions with equal magnitude momentum.

parts.prompt: Calculate the energy of each emitted gamma photon in MeV and its frequency in Hz.
parts.expectedAnswer: Each photon energy $= 0.651 MeV$; frequency $= 1.57 × 10²⁰ Hz$
workingSteps: Energy of each photon $E = E_0 + \frac{1}{2}E_{\text{k,tot}} = 0.651 MeV$.
Convert to joules and compute $f = E/h = 1.57 × 10²⁰ Hz$.

parts.prompt: Explain why two photons are emitted in opposite directions during annihilation.
parts.expectedAnswer: Initial momentum is approximately zero, so two gamma photons travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum.
workingSteps: State momentum conservation from near-zero initial momentum.
Conclude two identical photons travel in opposite directions (reject 'elimination').

items.stem: In Required Practical 12 with systematic offset $x_0 = 22$ mm, the background-corrected gamma count rate at ruler distance $x_1 = 140$ mm is 123 s⁻¹. Predict the corrected count rate at $x_2 = 420$ mm.
items.workedSolution: Background rate $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 480/(20\times 60) = 0.400 s⁻¹$. From $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}} = (x + x_0)/\sqrt{k}$, gradient $= 1/\sqrt{k} = 0.556$, so $k = 3.24 s⁻¹ m²$, $x_0 = \text{intercept}/\text{grad} = 22$ mm, and $C_{\mathrm{corr},2} = 16.6 s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines cCorr2 $= 16.6 s⁻¹$.

items.stem: A magnesium ion has two fewer orbital electrons than protons in its nucleus. Which statement correctly explains how to determine the specific charge of this ion rather than its bare nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Only the net uncompensated charge (+2e) determines $Q$, while all protons, neutrons (and remaining electrons) contribute to mass $m$. Therefore option C is correct: ion charge equals excess or deficit electrons while total mass includes all nucleons.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: ion charge equals excess or deficit electrons while total mass includes all nucleons.

items.stem: Why must electrons be accelerated to several hundred MeV (so λ ~ 10⁻¹⁵ m) to measure nuclear radii by diffraction, instead of using low-energy keV electrons?
items.workedSolution: Appreciable diffraction needs λ ~ R (~10⁻¹⁵ m), and high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound. Therefore the correct statement is: Diffraction requires de Broglie wavelength comparable to nuclear diameter (~10⁻¹⁵ m), and high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound.

options.label: A
options.text: Diffraction requires de Broglie wavelength comparable to nuclear diameter (~10⁻¹⁵ m), and high-energy electrons are leptons unaffected by the strong nuclear force and diffract to a non-zero first minimum giving radius directly, whereas alpha closest approach only gives an energy-dependent upper bound

options.label: B
options.text: Low-energy electrons are hadrons that get absorbed by the strong nuclear force before reaching the detector.
options.distractorRationale: Electrons are leptons at all energies and never feel the strong nuclear force.

options.label: C
options.text: High-energy electrons have much longer de Broglie wavelengths so sin θ stays larger than one.
options.distractorRationale: Higher momentum gives a SHORTER de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p, and sin θ must be < 1.

options.label: D
options.text: Low-energy electrons move faster than light and bypass the target nuclei completely.
options.distractorRationale: No massive particle exceeds c; low-energy electrons simply have λ >> R, giving no observable nuclear diffraction minimum.

items.stem: Why are newly discharged spent fuel rods stored underwater in deep cooling ponds for several years before vitrification and long-term disposal?
items.workedSolution: High-level radioactive fission fragments are handled remotely in cooling ponds, vitrified in glass inside steel canisters, and stored in deep geologically stable underground repositories. Therefore the correct statement is: Water provides both continuous cooling for decay heat and radiation shielding before high-level radioactive fission fragments are handled remotely in cooling ponds, vitrified in glass inside steel canisters, and stored in deep geologically stable underground repositories

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: high-level radioactive fission fragments are handled remotely in cooling ponds, vitrified in glass inside steel canisters, and stored in deep geologically stable underground repositories.

options.label: A
options.text: Water dissolves the uranium fuel chemically so all long-lived isotopes turn into stable lead within days.
options.distractorRationale: Water does not change nuclear half-lives; short-lived isotopes decay naturally while long-lived waste still requires vitrification.

options.label: B
options.text: Water freezes the fission fragments below zero kelvin to halt beta-minus decay permanently.
options.distractorRationale: Radioactive decay is spontaneous and completely independent of temperature.

options.label: C
options.text: Water provides both continuous cooling for decay heat and radiation shielding before high-level radioactive fission fragments are handled remotely in cooling ponds, vitrified in glass inside steel canisters, and stored in deep geologically stable underground repositories

options.label: D
options.text: Water converts high-level waste into low-level waste ready for open-air disposal within one week.
options.distractorRationale: High-level waste remains dangerous for thousands of years and requires deep geologically stable storage.

Calculate the duration of the $1.50\,\mu\text{s}$ onboard interval as measured by clocks on the space station.
State how the null result of the Michelson–Morley experiment supported the invariance of $c$ underlying these equations.
parts.expectedAnswer: The experiment recorded zero fringe shift on ninety degree rotation disproved absolute motion through an ether and supported invariant light speed.
workingSteps: Rotating the interferometer by $90°$ yielded zero fringe shift despite Earth's orbital motion.
This disproved a stationary ether and confirmed $c$ is identical along every direction.

items.stem: Particle-nuclear tracking in a proton-beam spallation iron-52 decay chain follows a iron parent (nucleon number 52, proton number 26) undergoing purely weak beta-plus transitions (u → d + e⁺ + νₑ) to form a daughter nucleus (A = 52, Z = 24).
items.workedSolution: (a) ΔZ = 24 − 26 = −2. Final answer: −2. (b) N₀ = 52 − 26 = 26; N_f = 52 − 24 = 28. ΔN = N_f − N₀ = 2. Final answer: 2. (c) Accounting for ΔA = 0, charge conservation gives 2 weak beta transitions. Final answer: 2.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Z_final − Z_parent with sign to obtain −2.
Computes N = A − Z for parent and daughter and takes N_final − N_parent.
Evaluates correctly to 2.
Links single-quark flavour conversion to ΔZ = ±1 per weak beta step.
Evaluates correctly to 2.

items.stem: During an experiment in a heavy-element Coulomb-barrier scattering rig, an alpha particle (charge +2e) of kinetic energy 3.6 MeV is directed along a head-on trajectory toward a fixed lead nucleus (proton number Z = 82, nucleon number A = 208). Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Eₖ = 3.6 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 5.76 × 10⁻¹³ J. d = k(2e)(82e) / Eₖ = 6.55 × 10⁻¹⁴ m = 65.5 fm. Final answer: 65.5 fm. (b) R = 1.20 × (208)^(1/3) = 7.11 fm (< d, confirming pure electrostatic scattering). Final answer: 7.11 fm. (c) ρ = (208 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷) / ((4/3)π(7.11 × 10⁻¹⁵)³) = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. Final answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

items.stem: Monochromatic light above threshold frequency strikes a photocathode, producing curve Q on the $I\text{–}V$ graph. The light intensity is increased at constant frequency to produce curve P. Which statement describes the resulting changes?
items.workedSolution: More photons per second liberate more electrons per second (higher saturation photocurrent), while $eV_{\text{s}} = hf - \phi$ is unchanged at fixed frequency. Therefore option A is correct: increasing intensity increases photocurrent while stopping potential remains unchanged.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: increasing intensity increases photocurrent while stopping potential remains unchanged.

options.label: A
options.text: At constant frequency above threshold, increasing intensity increases photocurrent while stopping potential remains unchanged

options.label: B
options.text: At constant frequency above threshold, doubling intensity doubles both photocurrent and stopping potential
options.distractorRationale: Classic AQA trap: intensity changes photon arrival rate (current), NOT individual photon energy hf or stopping potential Vs.

options.label: C
options.text: At constant frequency above threshold, photocurrent stays constant while stopping potential increases
options.distractorRationale: Confuses increasing intensity with increasing frequency at constant photon arrival rate.

options.label: D
options.text: At constant frequency above threshold, both photocurrent and stopping potential remain completely unchanged
options.distractorRationale: Higher intensity delivers more photons per second, liberating more photoelectrons per second.

items.stem: In an evacuated electron-diffraction tube, electrons accelerated from rest through 1300 V pass through sputtered polycrystalline silver film of interplanar spacing d = 2.36 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and form concentric bright rings on a phosphor screen L = 0.17 m behind the foil. Use sin θ = λ / d and ring radius r = L tan θ, taking h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) p = √(2mₑeV) = 1.95 × 10⁻²³ N s. λ = h / p = 3.41 × 10⁻¹¹ m = 34.1 pm. Final answer: 34.1 pm. (b) sin θ = λ / d = 3.41 × 10⁻¹¹ / (2.36 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) = 0.144. θ = 8.30 °. Final answer: 8.30 °. (c) r = L tan θ = 0.17 × tan(8.30°) = 0.0248 m. Final answer: 0.0248 m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ = h / √(2mₑeV) with SI values and converts to picometres.
Evaluates correctly to 34.1 pm.
Applies sin θ = λ / d and converts to degrees.
Evaluates correctly to 8.30 °.
Evaluates r = L tan θ using the screen distance L.
Evaluates correctly to 0.0248 m.

Model the nuclear radius as R = R₀ A^(1/3) with R₀ = 1.20 fm = 1.20 × 10⁻¹⁵ m and nucleon mass unit u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
items.workedSolution: (a) R = 1.20 × (120)^(1/3) = 5.92 fm. Final answer: 5.92 fm. (b) R = 5.92 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. Final answer: 5.92 × 10⁻¹⁵ m. (c) m = 120 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; V = (4/3)π(5.92 × 10⁻¹⁵)³. ρ = m / V = 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³. Final answer: 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes nucleon number A into R = R₀ A^(1/3).
Evaluates correctly to 5.92 fm.

Divides nuclear mass A u by spherical volume (4/3)πR³.
Evaluates correctly to 2.29 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.

items.stem: A vapour cell in a laser-cooled rubidium magnetometry cell contains rubidium vapour whose the first excited state lies at −2.63 eV and whose adjacent bound level lies at −4.27 eV relative to the continuum threshold. Assume h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What minimum photon frequency is required to ionize the atom from the first excited state?
items.workedSolution: Energy needed to reach the continuum is ΔE = 2.63 eV = 4.21 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Threshold frequency f = ΔE / h = 4.21 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 6.35 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

markScheme.criterion: Uses f = |E| e / h to obtain 6.35 × 10¹⁴ Hz (D).

items.stem: In a Scanning Tunnelling Microscope (STM), the sharp metal probe tip is held roughly one nanometre above a conducting sample with a small bias voltage far below the work function. How does a measurable current still cross the empty vacuum gap?
items.workedSolution: An electron's wavefunction penetrates the finite potential barrier so electrons cross the narrow vacuum gap by quantum tunnelling with current decaying exponentially as gap width increases.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that electrons cross the narrow vacuum gap by quantum tunnelling with current decaying exponentially as gap width increases.

items.stem: At a hospital nuclear-medicine dispenser, a Geiger–Müller tube measures a mean background count rate of 18 counts min⁻¹ with no sample present. When a technetium-99m source of half-life 6 h is placed in front of the window at t = 0, the total recorded count rate is 118 counts min⁻¹. The detector is read again at t = 12 h. What total count rate (including background) does the detector record at t = 12 h?
items.workedSolution: Initial net count rate C₀ = 118 − 18 = 100 counts min⁻¹. Number of half-lives n = 12 / 6 = 2. Remaining net count rate C = 100 / 2^2 = 25 counts min⁻¹. Total recorded count rate = 25 + 18 = 43.0 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background (100), divides by 2^2 (25), and adds 18 back to obtain 43.0 counts min⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides the initial total count rate directly by 2ⁿ without subtracting the background count rate first.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Correctly halves the background-subtracted net count rate but forgets to add the background count rate back to obtain the total detector reading.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Halves the uncorrected count rate first and subtracts the background count rate at the end.

items.stem: A freshly prepared vial in a weld-inspection gamma radiography vault contains N₀ = 4.3 × 10¹⁵ undecayed nuclei of iridium-192, whose half-life is 73.8 d. The vial is stored for t = 120 d before administration. What is the activity of the sample, in becquerels (Bq), at t = 120 d?
items.workedSolution: T₁/₂ = 73.8 × 86400 = 6.38 × 10⁶ s, so λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂ = 1.09 × 10⁻⁷ s⁻¹. Initial activity A₀ = λN₀ = 4.67 × 10⁸ Bq. At t = 120 d, A = A₀ e^(−λt) = 1.51 × 10⁸ Bq.

markScheme.criterion: Converts T₁/₂ to seconds, finds A₀ = λN₀, and evaluates A = A₀ e^(−λt) = 1.51 × 10⁸ Bq (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Fails to convert half-life from d to seconds (× 86400) when computing A = λN in Bq (s⁻¹).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the initial activity A₀ = λN₀ at t = 0 without multiplying by the exponential decay factor e^(−λt).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses λ = 1 / T₁/₂ instead of λ = ln 2 / T₁/₂ when converting half-life to decay constant.

items.stem: Referring to the subatomic particle classification chart, which statement about baryons is correct?
items.workedSolution: Every free baryon eventually decays into a proton; the proton is the only stable free baryon composed of three quarks ($uud$). Therefore option C is correct: proton is the only stable free baryon composed of three quarks.

markScheme.criterion: Select option C: proton is the only stable free baryon composed of three quarks.

items.stem: Electrons in a diffraction tube are accelerated from rest through an anode potential difference of $4200\text{ V}$. Using $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}$, $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, and $m_{\text{e}} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$, calculate their de Broglie wavelength in picometres.
items.workedSolution: $p = \sqrt{2m_{\text{e}}eV} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \times 4200} = 3.50 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹$, giving $\lambda = h/p = 18.9 pm$. Option A (18.9 pm) matches.

markScheme.criterion: de Broglie wavelength $= 18.9 pm$ (18.9 pm, option A).

items.stem: Radiative recombination diagnostics on an electron-beam ion-trap (EBIT) X-ray source analyse single-electron beryllium Be³⁺ (Z = 4) starting from outer bound shell n = 5 using Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV. Assume h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Eₙ = −13.6 × (4)² / (5)² = −8.70 eV. Ionization energy ΔE = 0 − Eₙ = 8.70 eV. Final answer: 8.70 eV. (b) ΔE = 8.70 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.39 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. f = ΔE / h = 1.39 × 10⁻¹⁸ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 2.10 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Final answer: 2.10 × 10¹⁵ Hz. (c) λ = (3.00 × 10⁸) / (2.10 × 10¹⁵) = 143 nm. Final answer: 143 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ΔE = 13.6 Z² / n² eV for the specified Z and n.
Evaluates correctly to 8.70 eV.
Converts ionization energy from eV to J and divides by Planck's constant h.
Evaluates correctly to 2.10 × 10¹⁵ Hz.
Uses λ = c / f and expresses the wavelength in nm to obtain 143 nm.

items.stem: A beam of electrons starts from rest in a low-energy electron diffraction (LEED) gun and accelerates through a potential difference of 3200 V in vacuum. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Eₖ = qV = 5.12 × 10⁻¹⁶ J. v = √(2Eₖ / m) = 3.35 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. Final answer: 3.35 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. (b) λ = h / (mv) = 2.17 × 10⁻¹¹ m = 0.0217 nm. Final answer: 0.0217 nm. (c) λ = 21.7 pm. Final answer: 21.7 pm.

markScheme.criterion: Equates ½mv² = qV and solves v = √(2qV / m).
Evaluates correctly to 3.35 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.
Divides Planck's constant h by mv and converts metres to nanometres.
Evaluates correctly to 0.0217 nm.
Multiplies wavelength in nm by 1000 pm nm⁻¹ to obtain 21.7 pm.

Determine the de Broglie wavelength, in nanometres (nm), of the beam.

items.stem: A radiographer increases the accelerating anode potential difference of a tungsten X-ray tube while keeping the filament current unchanged. How does the emitted X-ray intensity-versus-wavelength spectrum change?
items.workedSolution: Because $\lambda_{\min} = hc/(eV)$ and K-lines are fixed by atomic shell gaps, increasing anode voltage reduces minimum wavelength and raises intensity while characteristic peak wavelengths stay fixed.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies that increasing anode voltage reduces minimum wavelength and raises intensity while characteristic peak wavelengths stay fixed.

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing anode voltage shifts both minimum wavelength and tungsten K-line wavelengths shorter.
options.distractorRationale: Characteristic K-line wavelengths depend solely on tungsten atomic energy levels, not tube voltage.

options.label: B
options.text: Increasing anode voltage keeps minimum wavelength unchanged while raising only the peak height.
options.distractorRationale: Keeping cutoff fixed while raising height occurs when increasing filament current, not anode voltage.

options.label: C
options.text: Raising the tube voltage causes increasing anode voltage reduces minimum wavelength and raises intensity while characteristic peak wavelengths stay fixed.

options.label: D
options.text: Increasing anode voltage lengthens minimum wavelength because electrons lose more heat.
options.distractorRationale: Higher anode voltage gives greater maximum photon energy and therefore a shorter cutoff wavelength.

items.stem: Reaction kinematics in a mixed-oxide thermal reactor assembly examine molybdenum–tin fission of plutonium-239, where bare rest masses satisfy plutonium nucleus (239.0006 u) + 1 thermal neutron (1.008665 u) → tin-134 nucleus (133.8902 u) + ruthenium-103 nucleus (102.8825 u) + 3 neutrons (each 1.008665 u). Assume 1 u = 931.5 MeV c⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the rest-mass decrease Δm, in atomic mass units (u), in a single fission reaction?
items.workedSolution: Summing reactant and product rest masses gives Δm = Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 0.211 u.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 0.211 u (A).

items.stem: Monochromatic electromagnetic radiation of frequency 2.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz strikes an electroscope-mounted clean zinc UV plate whose work function is 4.33 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Φ = 4.33 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.93 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. f₀ = Φ / h = 6.93 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 1.04 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Final answer: 1.04 × 10¹⁵ Hz. (b) Photon energy E = hf / e = 10.4 eV. Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 10.4 − 4.33 = 6.03 eV. Final answer: 6.03 eV. (c) Vₛ = Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / e = 6.03 V. Final answer: 6.03 V.

markScheme.criterion: Converts Φ from eV to joules and applies f₀ = Φ / h.
Evaluates correctly to 1.04 × 10¹⁵ Hz.
Applies Einstein's photoelectric equation Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = hf/e − Φ.
Evaluates correctly to 6.03 eV.
Uses eVₛ = Eₖ,ₘₐₓ to obtain 6.03 V.

items.stem: Special-relativity timing in an astronomical interferometer frame follows a collimated microquasar plasmoid at speed v = 0.72c over an interstellar gas filament of proper length L₀ = 2.38 × 10¹⁰ m, given plasmoid-frame synchrotron flare duration Δt₀ = 85.8 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) γ = 1 / √(1 − 0.72²) = 1.44. Final answer: 1.44. (b) Δt = γ Δt₀ = 1.44 × 85.8 = 124 s. Final answer: 124 s. (c) L = L₀ / γ = 2.38 × 10¹⁰ / 1.44 = 1.65 × 10¹⁰ m. Final answer: 1.65 × 10¹⁰ m.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes β = v/c into γ = 1 / √(1 − β²).
Evaluates correctly to 1.44.
Multiplies proper time interval Δt₀ by γ (Δt = γ Δt₀).
Evaluates correctly to 124 s.
Divides proper length L₀ by γ (L = L₀ / γ).
Evaluates correctly to 1.65 × 10¹⁰ m.

items.stem: A high-energy gamma photon whose energy exceeds twice the rest energy of an electron undergoes pair production near a lead nucleus. What becomes of the energy in excess of the rest energies of the created pair?
items.workedSolution: By mass–energy conservation, any energy above $2E_0$ appears as kinetic energy of the created particles (AQA requires 'kinetic energy', not 'speed'). Therefore option D is correct: kinetic energy of the particles before annihilation or after pair creation.

markScheme.criterion: Select option D: kinetic energy of the particles before annihilation or after pair creation.

items.stem: Why does AQA Required Practical 12 recommend plotting $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against ruler distance $x$ rather than plotting $C_{\mathrm{corr}}$ against $1/x^2$, and what handling controls are essential?
items.workedSolution: RP12 mark-scheme precision: Plotting 1/√C_corr vs x stays linear with negative x-intercept −x₀ despite unknown internal offset; students must handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset.

options.label: A
options.text: Plotting C_corr against 1/x² always gives a straight line through the origin even with an unknown internal offset x₀.
options.distractorRationale: Because true distance is x + x₀, C_corr = k/(x + x₀)² curves significantly when plotted against 1/x².

options.label: B
options.text: Simply avoiding touching the source with bare fingers is a sufficient radiological safety protocol.
options.distractorRationale: AQA mark schemes explicitly reject bare 'do not touch'; specify long tongs, maximum distance, minimum exposure time, and lead-lined storage.

options.label: C
options.text: Plotting 1/√C_corr vs x eliminates the need to subtract background radiation.
options.distractorRationale: Background count rate MUST be subtracted before taking 1/√C_corr, otherwise the line bends horizontally at large x.

options.label: D
options.text: Plotting 1/√C_corr vs x stays linear with negative x-intercept −x₀ despite unknown internal offset; students must handle the sealed gamma source with long tongs maximise distance minimise exposure time outside lead storage and plot one over square root corrected count rate against x to reveal systematic offset.

items.stem: Using AQA nucleon masses ($m_{\text{p}} = 1.673 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, $m_{\text{n}} = 1.675 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$, $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$), calculate the magnitude of the specific charge of a bare $^{56}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}$ nucleus.
items.workedSolution: Net charge magnitude $Q = 26 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 4.16 × 10⁻¹⁸ C$ and mass $m = 9.37 × 10⁻²⁶ kg$, giving $Q/m = 4.44 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹$. Option A (4.44 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Correct specific charge $Q/m = 4.44 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹$ (4.44 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹, option A).

items.stem: A beam of 250 MeV electrons (λ ≈ hc / E) scatters off iron-56 nuclei, producing a non-zero first diffraction minimum at θ_min = 43.3° (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). Using sin θ ≈ 0.61 λ / R, calculate the nuclear radius R of iron-56 in femtometres.
items.workedSolution: λ = hc / E = 4.97 fm. Rearranging sin θ ≈ 0.61 λ / R gives R = 0.61 λ / sin(43.3°) = 4.40 fm.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates nuclear radius R = 4.40 fm.

items.stem: A linear particle accelerator tunnel has a proper length of 1500 m in the laboratory frame. What length does this tunnel appear to have in the rest frame of a particle moving through it at $0.800c$?
items.workedSolution: $\sqrt{1 - 0.800^2} = 0.600$, so contracted length is $l = l_0 \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} = 1500 \times 0.600 = 900 m$.

markScheme.criterion: Correct calculated value 900 m.

items.stem: During a positron-annihilation lifetime spectroscopy source, weak quark-flavour transitions (purely weak beta-plus transitions (u → d + e⁺ + νₑ)) convert a parent sodium nucleus with A = 22, Z = 11 into a product nucleus with A = 22, Z = 10. What is the signed net change in neutron number ΔN = N_final − N_parent across the sequence?
items.workedSolution: Initial neutron number N₀ = 22 − 11 = 11; final neutron number N_f = 22 − 10 = 12. Thus ΔN = N_f − N₀ = 1.

markScheme.criterion: Uses N = A − Z to obtain ΔN = (22 − 10) − (22 − 11) = 1 (A).

items.stem: Electrostatic repulsion inside a heavy-metal beam-diagnostics scattering foil halts a head-on proton (charge +1e) of initial energy 5.1 MeV at closest approach d from a stationary tantalum nucleus (Z = 73, A = 181). Assume k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the distance of closest approach d, in femtometres (fm)?
items.workedSolution: Initial kinetic energy Eₖ = 5.1 × 10⁶ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 8.16 × 10⁻¹³ J. At the turning point, Eₖ = k(1e)(73e) / d, so d = (8.99 × 10⁹)(1)(73)(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹)² / 8.16 × 10⁻¹³ = 20.6 fm.

markScheme.criterion: Equates Eₖ to k Q₁ Q₂ / d to obtain d = 20.6 fm (D).

items.stem: Nuclear stability mapping of an alpha-proton X-ray spectrometer source connects parent curium (A = 244, Z = 96) to product nuclide (A = 228, Z = 90) through a series consisting strictly of alpha and beta-minus emissions. How many beta-minus particles are emitted in this decay sequence?
items.workedSolution: Only alpha decay changes nucleon number A: Nα = (244 − 228) / 4 = 4. Proton balance gives 90 = 96 − 2(4) + Nβ⁻, so Nβ⁻ = 90 − 88 = 2.

markScheme.criterion: Finds Nα = 4 from ΔA / 4 and solves Z_f = Z_0 − 2Nα + Nβ⁻ to obtain Nβ⁻ = 2 (D).

items.stem: Which statement is the exact AQA definition of the work function $\phi$ of a metal?
items.workedSolution: AQA requires both 'minimum energy' and 'metal surface': minimum energy required to remove an electron from the metal surface. Therefore option C is correct: minimum energy required to remove an electron from the metal surface.

items.stem: Electrons accelerated from rest by a 4450 V supply diffract through evaporated polycrystalline gold film with lattice spacing d = 2.35 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, producing a circular first-order ring on a screen at distance L = 0.15 m. Given sin θ = λ / d, r = L tan θ, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C: What is the radius r of the first-order bright diffraction ring on the screen?
items.workedSolution: λ = h / √(2mₑeV) = 1.84 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Then sin θ = λ / d = 0.0783, giving θ = 4.49 ° and ring radius r = L tan θ = 0.15 × tan(4.49°) = 0.0118 m.

markScheme.criterion: Finds λ = 1.84 × 10⁻¹¹ m, θ = 4.49°, and r = L tan θ = 0.0118 m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the full diameter 2r of the diffraction ring instead of its radius r.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 inside p = √(2mₑeV), overestimating λ and ring radius by √2.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the diffraction ratio as d / λ instead of λ / d.

items.stem: Spectroscopic analysis of rubidium vapour in a laser-cooled rubidium magnetometry cell places the first excited state at −2.59 eV and a neighbouring bound state at −4.18 eV, taking free electrons at rest to have zero energy. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) ΔE = 0 − (−2.59) = 2.59 eV. Final answer: 2.59 eV. (b) ΔE = 2.59 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. f = ΔE / h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) = 6.25 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Final answer: 6.25 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (c) λ = c / f = (3.00 × 10⁸) / (6.25 × 10¹⁴) = 4.80 × 10⁻⁷ m. Converting to nanometres gives λ = 480 nm. Final answer: 480 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Finds ΔE = 0 − E_initial in eV to obtain 2.59 eV.
Converts ΔE to joules (× 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) and applies f = ΔE / h.
Evaluates correctly to 6.25 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
Uses λ = c / f (or hc / ΔE) and converts metres to nanometres.
Evaluates correctly to 480 nm.

items.stem: In electron capture, an inner-shell atomic electron interacts with a nuclear proton as illustrated. Which exchange particle and direction correctly complete the diagram?
items.workedSolution: In electron capture, the proton emits a $W^+$ boson to become a neutron, and the electron absorbs $W^+$ to become $\nu_e$. Therefore option A is correct: W plus boson from proton to electron.

markScheme.criterion: Select option A: W plus boson from proton to electron.

parts.prompt: Calculate the fractional factor $I / I_0$ and the new tunnelling current when the surface drops by $\Delta d = 0.150\text{ nm}$.
Explain why quantum tunnelling enables an STM to detect height variations far smaller than a single atomic diameter.
parts.expectedAnswer: Because electrons cross the narrow vacuum gap by quantum tunnelling with current decaying exponentially as gap width increases, even a sub-atomic change in gap produces a large fractional change in measured current.
workingSteps: Electron wavefunctions decay exponentially across the vacuum potential barrier.
Hence tiny vertical height steps cause dramatic, easily measurable shifts in tunnelling current.

items.stem: At a positron-imaging elution calibrator, a Geiger–Müller tube measures a mean background count rate of 18 counts min⁻¹ with no sample present. When a gallium-68 source of half-life 68 min is placed in front of the window at t = 0, the total recorded count rate is 418 counts min⁻¹. The detector is read again at t = 272 min.
items.workedSolution: (a) C₀,net = 418 − 18 = 400 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 400 counts min⁻¹. (b) n = 272 / 68 = 4 half-lives. C_net = 400 / 2^4 = 25.0 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 25.0 counts min⁻¹. (c) C_total = 25 + 18 = 43.0 counts min⁻¹. Final answer: 43.0 counts min⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts background count rate from initial total count rate to obtain 400 counts min⁻¹.
Identifies 4 elapsed half-lives and divides initial net count rate by 2^4.
Evaluates correctly to 25.0 counts min⁻¹.
Adds background count rate back to the remaining net count rate to obtain 43.0 counts min⁻¹.

Evaluates correctly to 7.77 × 10¹⁰ Bq.
Applies exponential decay law A = A₀ e^(−λt) with consistent time units.
Evaluates correctly to 1.10 × 10¹⁰ Bq.

items.stem: A negative kaon ($K^-$, quark composition $s\bar{u}$, strangeness $S = -1$) decays into two pions: $K^- \to \pi^- + \pi^0$. Calculate the change in strangeness $\Delta S = S_{\text{after}} - S_{\text{before}}$.
items.workedSolution: Before decay $S = -1$ ($K^-$); after decay $S = 0 + 0 = 0$ ($\pi^-$ and $\pi^0$). Thus $\Delta S = 0 - (-1) = +1.00$. Option A (1.00) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Change in strangeness $\Delta S = +1$ (1.00, option A).

items.stem: Why is the inner glass surface of a low-pressure mercury fluorescent tube coated with a white phosphor powder?
items.workedSolution: Excited mercury atoms emit high-energy UV photons; the phosphor coating absorbs ultraviolet photons and de-excites in multiple smaller steps emitting visible light. Therefore option B is correct: phosphor coating absorbs ultraviolet photons and de excites in multiple smaller steps emitting visible light.

markScheme.criterion: Select option B: phosphor coating absorbs ultraviolet photons and de excites in multiple smaller steps emitting visible light.

options.label: C
options.text: The coating is needed because the phosphor speeds up free electrons to higher kinetic energies

items.stem: Radiative recombination diagnostics on an electron-beam ion-trap (EBIT) X-ray source analyse single-electron beryllium Be³⁺ (Z = 4) starting from outer bound shell n = 5 using Eₙ = −13.6 Z² / n² eV. Assume h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the series-limit (maximum) photon wavelength that can photoionize this species from outer bound shell n = 5?
items.workedSolution: Initial level energy Eₙ = −13.6 × 4² / 5² = −8.70 eV. Ionization requires ΔE = 8.70 eV = 1.39 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. Maximum ionizing wavelength λ = hc / ΔE = 143 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Computes ΔE = 13.6 Z² / n² eV and λ = hc / ΔE = 143 nm (B).

items.stem: To benchmark nuclear stability in a supernova core stability-peak measurement, consider a bare iron-56 nucleus of nucleon number A = 56, proton number Z = 26, and nuclear mass 55.920674 u (mₚ = 1.007276 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u, u = 931.5 MeV c⁻²). What is the binding energy per nucleon, in MeV, of this iron-56 nucleus?
items.workedSolution: Neutron count N = 56 − 26 = 30. Mass defect Δm = 26(1.007276) + 30(1.008665) − 55.920674 = 0.528 u. Total binding energy B = Δm × 931.5 = 492 MeV. Binding energy per nucleon B / A = 492 / 56 = 8.79 MeV.

markScheme.criterion: Computes Δm = 0.528 u, B = 492 MeV, and B / A = 8.79 MeV (A).

items.stem: A beam of protons starts from rest in a surface-analysis proton microprobe injector and accelerates through a potential difference of 220 V in vacuum. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₚ = 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the de Broglie wavelength, in picometres (pm), of the protons?
items.workedSolution: Kinetic energy Eₖ = qV = 3.52 × 10⁻¹⁷ J. Momentum p = √(2mEₖ) = 3.43 × 10⁻²² N s. De Broglie wavelength λ = h / p = 1.93 pm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates p and λ = h / p to obtain 1.93 pm (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 2 inside p = √(2mEₖ), computing λ = h / √(mEₖ).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the elementary charge factor e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C when converting accelerating voltage to joules.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats the massive particle as a massless photon using λ = hc / E instead of λ = h / p.

items.stem: Energy-balance modelling of an electrostatic-confinement D–³He fusion chamber considers deuterium–helium-3 aneutronic fusion: deuteron (2.013553 u) + helium-3 nucleus (3.014932 u) → alpha particle (4.001506 u) + proton (1.007276 u). Use u = 931.5 MeV c⁻² and elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.workedSolution: (a) Δm = Σm_reactants − Σm_products = 0.0197 u. Final answer: 0.0197 u. (b) Q = 0.0197 × 931.5 = 18.4 MeV. Final answer: 18.4 MeV. (c) Total nucleon number A = 5. Final answer: 5.

markScheme.criterion: Sums all reactant and product rest masses including particle multiplicities.
Evaluates correctly to 0.0197 u.
Multiplies Δm in u by 931.5 MeV u⁻¹.
Evaluates correctly to 18.4 MeV.
Sums nucleon numbers across reactants (or products) to obtain 5.

items.stem: Monochromatic electromagnetic radiation of frequency 6.16 × 10¹⁴ Hz strikes an evacuated caesium-antimonide night-vision photocell whose work function is 1.95 eV. Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What reverse stopping potential Vₛ is required to reduce the collector photocurrent to zero?
items.workedSolution: Photon energy E = hf / e = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 6.16 × 10¹⁴) / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 2.55 eV. Maximum kinetic energy Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = E − Φ = 2.55 − 1.95 = 0.603 eV. Hence stopping potential Vₛ = 0.603 V.

markScheme.criterion: Computes eVₛ = hf − Φ to obtain Vₛ = 0.603 V (D).

items.stem: Within two stationary relay towers, a deep-space relativistic courier vessel maintain speed v = 0.84c across the inter-beacon corridor whose proper length is L₀ = 5.04 × 10⁹ m; their onboard telemetry cycle duration is Δt₀ = 19.6 s. What contracted length L of the baseline L₀ is measured in the moving rest frame?
items.workedSolution: Lorentz factor γ = 1 / √(1 − 0.84²) = 1.84. Contracted length L = L₀ / γ = 5.04 × 10⁹ / 1.84 = 2.73 × 10⁹ m.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates γ = 1.84 and L = L₀ / γ = 2.73 × 10⁹ m (A).

items.stem: An excimer UV laser operating at wavelength 148 nm irradiates a freshly cleaved lithium vacuum target (lithium work function 2.93 eV). Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. What is the maximum speed of the emitted photoelectrons?
items.workedSolution: Incident photon energy E = hc / λ = 1.34 × 10⁻¹⁸ J; work function Φ = 2.93 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.69 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Thus Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = 8.75 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, giving vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ) = 1.39 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes Eₖ,ₘₐₓ = hc/λ − Φ and vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ,ₘₐₓ / mₑ) = 1.39 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: A gamma photon of energy $1.64\text{ MeV}$ undergoes electron–positron pair production near a heavy nucleus. Given that each particle has rest energy $0.511\text{ MeV}$, calculate the total kinetic energy of the created electron and positron.
items.workedSolution: $E_{\text{k,tot}} = E_\gamma - 2E_0 = 1.64 - 2(0.511) = 0.618 MeV$. Option C (0.618 MeV) matches.

markScheme.criterion: Total kinetic energy $= 0.618 MeV$ (0.618 MeV, option C).

items.stem: In Required Practical 12, a student plots $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}}$ against measured ruler distance $x$ (in m) and obtains a straight line of gradient 0.500 s^{1/2} m⁻¹ and vertical intercept 9.00 × 10⁻³ s^{1/2}. Calculate the hidden systematic offset distance $x_0$ inside the source and GM tube (in mm).
items.workedSolution: Background rate $C_{\mathrm{bg}} = 540/(20\times 60) = 0.450 s⁻¹$. From $1/\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{corr}}} = (x + x_0)/\sqrt{k}$, gradient $= 1/\sqrt{k} = 0.500$, so $k = 4.00 s⁻¹ m²$, $x_0 = \text{intercept}/\text{grad} = 18$ mm, and $C_{\mathrm{corr},2} = 18.3 s⁻¹$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly determines sourceOffsetX0Mm $= 18.0 mm$.
